description_full: Students follow the path from basic scientific discovery to clinical application. Hands-on laboratory work, interactive seminars, and visits to Dartmouth research settings introduce the methods and institutions that help move an idea from the laboratory bench to patient care. Students practice microscopy and micropipetting, examine cell division, diagnose a sickle cell case through gel electrophoresis, test enzyme activity in a catalase lab, and compare brain structures in a preserved sheep brain dissection. A zebrafish lab visit introduces model organisms and confocal microscopy. Two visits to Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center extend the investigation into chemistry and microbiology labs, pathology, clinical simulation, genomics, and medical imaging. Students also examine clinical trials, regulation, research ethics, and the responsibilities involved in human and animal research. In teams of two or three, students choose a cutting-edge medical topic, find both primary and reputable secondary sources, and create a visual and oral presentation. The project asks them to explain the most important findings clearly and connect the topic with the bench-to-bedside process. This two-week full-day academy is part of Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed and academically led by Dartmouth.

curriculum_sections.body: • Practice microscopy, micropipetting, and laboratory documentation • Diagnose a sickle cell case through gel electrophoresis • Test enzyme activity and examine cell division • Visit a zebrafish lab and learn about model organisms • Participate in a preserved sheep brain dissection • Tour pathology, genomics, imaging, and other facilities at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center • Research and present a cutting-edge medical topic with a team

curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Demonstrate foundational laboratory techniques and accurate scientific documentation • Explain how biomedical discoveries move from research toward patient care • Synthesize credible sources and present core findings from a team research project Students leave with laboratory records and a collaborative research presentation, stronger scientific literacy, and clearer direction about medicine, biomedical science, clinical research, or biotechnology.

Participants should be ready to follow laboratory safety directions, keep careful records, read scientific sources, collaborate on a research project, and discuss human and animal research ethics. The course includes preserved specimens and a sheep brain dissection; students who are concerned about these activities should speak with the instructor early. Closed-toe shoes are required in laboratory spaces.

description_full: How do you make a convincing point when every word, response, and cultural cue matters? Students strengthen spoken Spanish through the Rassias Method, which uses dramatic techniques, rhythmic drills, rapid reinforcement, and an error-tolerant classroom to encourage natural speech. Lead classes, reinforcement sessions, group lunches in Spanish, cultural programming, debates, negotiations, and presentations place grammar and vocabulary inside active communication. Students practice forming arguments, responding to counterarguments, and adapting persuasive choices to Spanish-speaking contexts. The emphasis stays on oral comprehension and spontaneous speech. Because the method depends on frequent participation, students keep returning to the language under different conditions. A phrase first practiced in a drill may reappear in a discussion, negotiation, cultural session, or unscripted response. The academy builds toward an approximately 15-minute verbal presentation on a topic each student has studied or cares about, followed by questions and answers. Students must organize an argument, speak with clarity, and respond in the moment. This two-week, full-day intensive academy is part of Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars in Hanover, New Hampshire. The academy is fully developed and run by Dartmouth and taught by Dartmouth faculty and expert instructors. Residential and commuter students participate throughout the day, pairing focused academic work with campus life and growing independence.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Leverage a unique method, Rassias, which was developed by Dartmouth to quicken learning • Build persuasive vocabulary for business, politics, law, and leadership • Practice spontaneous Spanish during dialogues, discussions, and group lunches • Form and defend arguments in debates, negotiations, and presentations • Respond to counterarguments and questions in real time • Adapt persuasive choices to Spanish-speaking cultural contexts • Deliver an approximately 15-minute verbal presentation with questions and answers

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Communicate persuasively in spoken Spanish using relevant vocabulary and rhetorical strategies • Formulate arguments and respond to questions or counterarguments in real time • Deliver a sustained verbal presentation adapted to a Spanish-speaking context Students leave with a completed oral presentation, stronger fluency and intercultural communication skills, and clearer direction about continued Spanish study and globally oriented fields.

It is especially relevant to students interested in language, culture, debate, public speaking, international relations, business, law, leadership, or global service. Participants should be ready to speak often, join rapid drills, make mistakes, respond to classmates, and present in Spanish. The source does not state a formal proficiency prerequisite. Students should expect an oral-intensive environment focused more on listening and speaking than on extended reading or writing.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Communicate persuasively in spoken Spanish using relevant vocabulary and rhetorical strategies • Formulate arguments and respond to questions or counterarguments in real time • Deliver a sustained verbal presentation adapted to a Spanish-speaking context Students leave with a completed oral presentation, stronger fluency and intercultural communication skills, and clearer direction about continued Spanish study and globally oriented fields.

title: The Dartmouth Leadership Institute
subject: Business, Leadership & Entrepreneurship

description_short: Leadership is often treated as a title. Dartmouth’s signature Leadership Institute treats it as a practice: understand yourself, earn trust, make decisions under uncertainty, and help a team move forward. description_full: Leadership is often treated as a title. Dartmouth’s signature Leadership Institute treats it as a practice: understand yourself, earn trust, make decisions under uncertainty, and help a team move forward. Students begin on Dartmouth campus with leadership models, neuroscience, self-assessments, values work, case examples, and guided discussion that reveal how strengths, habits, and choices shape a group. They then practice communication, teamwork, resilience, and judgment through collaborative challenges and write a personal This I Believe leadership essay. During the second week, the classroom expands to Dartmouth’s Moosilauke Ravine Lodge, a setting connected to generations of Dartmouth students. Hiking, orienteering, team initiatives, trail work, and increasingly complex outdoor challenges make leadership visible: students must decide when to step forward, when to listen, how to adapt, and how to support others. Reflection after each experience turns action into a personal framework for continued growth. That combination of intensive study, place-based challenge, and reflection is unique within the Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars portfolio. Students leave with real examples of leadership—not simply a claim that they are leaders—that they can draw on in college essays, interviews, internship materials, and early job applications. In feedback from students who took the course, 98% said they would use the program in their college applications, and 93% said they would recommend it to a friend. This is a two-week, full-day academy. The academy is available to residential students and will take place both on Dartmouth's main campus as well as the legendary mountain retreat, Moosilauke Ravine Lodge, where outdoor experiences become part of the learning and development. Fully developed and run by Dartmouth, it is taught by Dartmouth faculty and expert instructors.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Explore leadership models, personal values, and real-world examples of decision making • Identify your strengths, habits, and growth priorities through self-assessment programs • Build communication, teamwork, resilience, and decision-making through group challenges • Define and develop your emerging leadership philosophy in a This I Believe essay • Expand the classroom at Moosilauke lodge—a Dartmouth tradition for generations—through hiking, navigation and team challenges • Translate feedback into personal leadership strengths and development priorities • Leave with a personalized growth framework with evidence, goals, and next steps

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Articulate a personal leadership philosophy grounded in values, leadership concepts, and reflection • Apply communication, collaboration, and decision-making strategies in classroom and outdoor challenges • Use a leadership essay and personal growth framework to demonstrate evidence of personal growth Students leave with a finished This I Believe essay, a personal leadership framework, and concrete experiences they can draw on in college, internship, and early job applications or interviews.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for motivated high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade, whether they already lead clubs and teams or are only beginning to see themselves as leaders. It is a strong fit across public policy, business, medicine, engineering, environmental studies, the arts, and community advocacy because every field depends on communication, judgment, and collaboration. No prior formal leadership experience is required. Students should be ready to participate fully in outdoor activities including hiking, orienteering and trail work. They should be ready to engage in group initiatives, personal writing, guided reflection, and constructive feedback. The experience rewards curiosity, self-awareness, resilience, and a willingness to contribute when conditions change.

description_full: Students investigate how genetic variation contributes to inherited disorders, complex disease, and differences in treatment. Case studies and current scientific literature provide a path into inheritance patterns, gene-environment interactions, genomics, and genetic testing. The course connects biological mechanisms with the growing field of precision medicine. Students examine how genomic information can support prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, then read primary research to determine what a study found and what remains uncertain. Scientific progress also raises social and ethical questions. Discussions of benefits, risks, privacy, access, and the effects of genetic knowledge ask students to consider how rapidly advancing technologies should be used. A visit to the Genomics Shared Resource Lab and a guest research perspective connect the work to current practice. The academy asks students to move carefully between a genetic association, a biological explanation, and a possible medical use. That distinction helps them recognize both the potential of genomics and the uncertainty that must accompany responsible interpretation. This two-week, full-day intensive academy is part of Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars in Hanover, New Hampshire. The academy is fully developed and run by Dartmouth and taught by Dartmouth faculty and expert instructors. Residential and commuter students participate throughout the day, pairing focused academic work with campus life and growing independence.

Students examine happiness, resilience, and human flourishing through positive psychology, neuroscience, sociology, and behavioral science. Research discussions, reflective journaling, and experiential activities introduce gratitude, purpose, motivation, relationships, mindfulness, emotional intelligence, optimism, and resilience. Students evaluate evidence, question common misconceptions, and consider how individual habits and social conditions can influence well-being. As students move between research and reflection, they consider where evidence is persuasive, where questions remain open, and why a practice may not affect every person in the same way. Personal experience becomes something to examine, not universal proof. The academy connects scientific analysis with thoughtful reflection. Students test evidence-based practices, examine their own values and goals, and communicate psychological concepts without turning one strategy into a universal prescription. description_full: How can an object reveal the life of a person who used it long ago? Students practice the archaeologist’s core move: observing carefully before making an inference. Mystery bags, artifact descriptions, and replica-making challenges show how shape, material, context, and missing information affect an interpretation. Hands-on investigations include creating clay vessels or figurines, designing hieroglyphic stories, mapping a familiar or imagined place with symbols, and testing tool shapes through a bird-beak experiment. Students compare evidence, record what they notice, and explain why one conclusion is better supported than another. Activities also explore how early people solved problems with available natural materials. For the capstone, students select an archaeological question or site concept and assemble evidence into a poster, map, model, or exhibit-style presentation. They label observations and inferences separately, explain the limits of the evidence, and share what additional information would strengthen their conclusion. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus. The course is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students connect engaging academic exploration with campus life, new friendships, growing confidence, and curiosity about what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Use artifact features and context to make a supported inference about the past • Create maps, models, and records that document archaeological evidence • Present an interpretation while explaining uncertainty and missing information Students will leave with replica artifacts, field-style records, and a capstone display showing how evidence can be used to reconstruct part of the human past.

A strong participant brings curiosity, patience, and a willingness to revise. The most important preparation is readiness to ask questions and take part.

description_full: Children are already experts at asking why. Big Questions Club gives that curiosity a place to grow through stories, puzzles, mystery objects, movement, drawing, and role-play. As students explore questions about fairness, friendship, rules, and how we know what is true, they learn to explain what they think, listen to different ideas, and discover how a thoughtful question can lead somewhere unexpected. Each day turns one big idea into something students can see and do. Students might act out ways to share materials, follow instructions like a paper robot, sort clues to decide what can be known, or build a gallery around what makes something beautiful. They can participate through speaking, drawing, acting, or building. In the final week, each student chooses a favorite question and creates a Big Questions Gallery project. A poster, comic, model, or interactive display presents two possible answers, the student’s current view, and the reasons behind it. Students also complete an illustrated philosophy journal and share their finished work. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus. It is available to commuter students. description_full: Why does a plant have tall stems, purple flowers or jagged leaves? Students begin with real plants and seeds, then investigate the tiny instructions behind those visible traits. They plant fast-growing seeds, track changes in a journal and watch colored water travel through celery stems. The class moves from plant parts into genetics. Students extract DNA from strawberries, build a double-helix model with paired bases and compare inherited traits with learned traits. They open soaked beans to find the embryo, seed coat and cotyledon, explore pollination and group plants into families by shared features. Each student invents a plant with its own DNA pattern, traits, habitat and helpful mutation. They develop the idea through capstone checkpoints, rehearse their explanation and present the finished model during a Plant Genetics Showcase. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus. The course is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students connect engaging academic exploration with a welcoming campus community, growing confidence, and curiosity students can carry into what they explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how DNA carries instructions that influence plant traits • Observe plant growth and record evidence using drawings and simple descriptions • Create and present a model that connects DNA, traits, mutations and habitat Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a plant journal, a double-helix model and an original plant capstone that may spark more questions about genetics and the natural world.

description_full: Which paper airplane flies farthest? Is there really more of one candy color in the bag? Students become data detectives, using numbers as clues to answer questions through games and hands-on experiments. They sort candies, measure rolling balls, compare basketball scores, and test their predictions with classmates. The discoveries take shape in colorful graphs and simple tables. Students explore averages, middle values, and numbers that appear most often, then notice how much results change from one try to the next. Dice and spinner games introduce chance. Class surveys show how asking a question differently can change someone’s answer, while weather observations reveal patterns over time. For their final detective project, students choose something they want to find out. They make a prediction, gather information, create graphs, and share what they discovered. The fun is in following the clues, finding surprises, and explaining the answer in their own words. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus in Fairfield, Connecticut. The course is available to commuter students. Beyond class, children make new friends, enjoy campus activities, and build confidence trying something new.

description_full: The ocean connects tiny plankton, enormous marine mammals, coastal communities, and the global climate. Students investigate life from coral reefs to the ocean floor while asking how organisms are adapted to water, food webs, temperature, depth, and one another. Experiments and research make ocean systems tangible. Students test density, model the water cycle, examine ocean chemistry, and compare evolutionary and ecological relationships among marine plants and animals. They research a chosen organism, communicate its adaptations, and consider how temperature change, pollution, fishing, habitat loss, or other human activity may affect it. For the capstone, students investigate a marine issue and its effects on local animals, plants, and people. They propose a solution designed to benefit both communities and the environment, then plan how it could gain funding, supplies, or public support. A mock-election presentation asks them to defend the evidence and practicality behind the proposal. description_full: What makes a machine a robot? Students compare familiar robots, investigate the jobs they perform, and identify the sensors, instructions, movement, and feedback that allow a robot to act. A human “robot and programmer” activity shows why precise commands matter before students move into block-based coding. Using Microsoft MakeCode and Finch robots, students create sequences, control motion, test lights and sound, and adjust programs after observing what the robot actually does. Challenges include drawing geometric paths, measuring movement, and using code to reproduce patterns. Students learn to break a larger goal into smaller steps and debug one variable at a time. The capstone combines programming and creative engineering. Students develop an interactive Finch performance or art challenge inspired by activities such as the bee waggle dance and Mondrian-style drawing. They plan the behavior, write and test the code, document revisions, and demonstrate how the robot responds to their instructions. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus. The course is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students connect engaging academic exploration with campus life, new friendships, growing confidence, and curiosity about what students may want to explore next. description_full: Can the steps in an experiment work like instructions for a computer? Students explore that connection by building a paper rocket, planning a fair test and collecting data. Then they turn the same ideas about steps and variables into an algorithm and begin coding in Scratch. New investigations bring a different science challenge and a new coding skill. Students test hovercrafts on different surfaces, build paddle boats to study force and motion, use a chemical reaction to inflate a balloon and compare bubble solutions. Along the way, they create sprites, scrolling backgrounds, timers, platform games and chase games. For the capstone, each student chooses an experiment and turns it into an animated Scratch story. A storyboard guides the project, while custom sprites, changing backgrounds, speech or sound and code blocks bring the scientific method to life. Students share the final animation and explain their choices. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus. The course is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students connect engaging academic exploration with a welcoming campus community, growing confidence, and curiosity students can carry into what they explore next.

description_full: Why does the Moon seem to change shape, and how can a shadow reveal Earth’s movement? Students begin as sky detectives, recording wonder questions in a space journal and using spheres, flashlights, star maps, and simple observations to explore patterns they can see. Next, the class moves outward. Students create a walkable solar-system model, compare rocky planets and giant worlds, test how impacts form craters, and design a rover or lander for the conditions on a chosen planet or moon. A light-and-orbit demonstration introduces how astronomers discover planets beyond our solar system. The final week brings stars, galaxies, and the scale of the universe into view through image sorting, sequencing, art, and nesting models. Teams create a Space Discovery Museum exhibit with a model or interactive visual, labeled explanation, surprising fact, and short presentation. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus. It is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students connect hands-on learning with a welcoming campus day, new friendships, growing confidence, and curiosity students can keep exploring.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Record sky questions, observations, and drawings in a space journal • Model day, night, shadows, and Moon phases with light and spheres • Build a walkable model of the solar system • Test crater formation and redesign a planetary rover or lander • Compare star colors, stellar life cycles, and galaxy shapes • Create and present a Space Discovery Museum exhibit

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain selected sky patterns using observations and simple models • Compare planets, stars, and galaxies using age-appropriate evidence • Construct and present a model that communicates an astronomy idea Students will leave with a space journal, hands-on models, and a museum exhibit, along with new astronomy skills and curiosity to keep exploring.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for elementary school students who have completed 1st, 2nd, or 3rd grade and ask big questions about the Moon, planets, stars, or space travel. It welcomes children who enjoy drawing, building, observing, pretending, or sharing surprising facts. Students should be ready to work with classmates, use simple tools and materials, record ideas with words or pictures, and explain a model during a supportive final presentation. View the eligibility requirements for the Institute for the Gifted on our FAQ page. A completed program application is required.

Creative engineering adds a second challenge: a model must stand, move, or communicate an idea. Students sketch, build, test, and improve three-dimensional characters and story elements. Checkpoints guide topic choice, character development, plot, construction, and rehearsal. Students present the finished story, demonstrate the model, and explain how design decisions support the character and narrative. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus. The course is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students connect engaging academic exploration with a welcoming campus community, growing confidence, and curiosity students can carry into what they explore next.

Along the way, they use ideas from science, engineering, math, and art to plan and create original designs. Students investigate anc
description_full: A toothpick tower must stand tall without toppling. A pizza-box oven must capture enough heat to work. Students tackle playful challenges like these by taking objects apart, putting them together, and thinking with their hands. Along the way, they use ideas from science, engineering, math, and art to plan and create original designs. Students investigate ancient and modern engineering wonders and explore how chemical, civil, electrical, and mechanical engineers solve different problems. Geometry helps them plan structures, while experiments with heat, materials, and physical forces show how a design behaves. Each challenge gives students a chance to build, test, notice what happened, and try again. For the capstone, students choose a real-world concern connected to one of the engineering branches they explored. They design a solution as a model, prototype, detailed blueprint, or original product, then explain their engineering choices to classmates. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus in Fairfield, Connecticut. The program is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students take part in campus activities, make new friends, and build confidence trying something new.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Take apart and reassemble objects to investigate how they work • Explore ancient and modern engineering wonders • Use geometry to design and build a toothpick tower • Apply heat-energy concepts while creating a pizza-box oven • Compare chemical, civil, electrical, and mechanical engineering • Design and present a solution to a real-world concern

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply a build-test-improve process to an engineering challenge • Explain how geometry, heat, materials, or physical forces affect a design • Present a model, prototype, blueprint, or product that addresses a real-world concern Students will leave with hands-on challenge work and an original capstone solution that reflects new engineering skills and curiosity to keep creating.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for elementary school students who have completed 1st, 2nd, or 3rd grade and enjoy building, taking things apart, drawing plans, experimenting, or asking how everyday objects work. It is a good fit for curious makers who want to try several kinds of engineering through hands-on challenges. No prerequisites are required. Students should be ready to share materials, work with classmates, follow instructions for classroom tools, and keep trying when a design needs improvement. Students must bring a laptop or compatible tablet, a charger, and compatible headphones. View the eligibility requirements for the Institute for the Gifted on our FAQ page.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply a build-test-improve process to an engineering challenge • Explain how geometry, heat, materials, or physical forces affect a design • Present a model, prototype, blueprint, or product that addresses a real-world concern Students will leave with hands-on challenge work and an original capstone solution that reflects new engineering skills and curiosity to keep creating.

title: Advanced Debate: Persuasive Public Speaking
subject: Humanities

description_short: What makes an argument persuasive when the stakes are high? Students examine how structure, evidence, word choice, voice, pacing, and body language influence an audience. description_full: What makes an argument persuasive when the stakes are high? Students examine how structure, evidence, word choice, voice, pacing, and body language influence an audience. Short speaking games and low-pressure speeches give them repeated opportunities to organize ideas, test delivery choices, and respond to focused feedback. The course moves from individual speaking to structured argument. Students develop claims, reasons, evidence, counterarguments, and rebuttals, then practice cross-examination and respectful questioning. Argument maps help teams see where a position is strong, where evidence is missing, and how an opposing side may respond. Students also learn how judges evaluate clarity, logic, listening, and fairness. A final team debate brings the process together. Students prepare roles, research support, draft questions and closing statements, complete practice rounds, and revise before presenting. Every student contributes as a speaker, debater, or judge, applying persuasive communication while listening carefully and disagreeing with respect. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Organize short speeches with clear openings, evidence, and conclusions • Practice posture, eye contact, pacing, tone, and audience awareness • Build argument maps from claims, reasons, and supporting evidence • Develop respectful rebuttals and cross-examination questions • Apply a scoring template while serving as a debate judge • Prepare and participate in a structured final team debate

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Organize and deliver a persuasive speech for a defined audience • Construct and defend an evidence-based argument while addressing counterclaims • Evaluate a debate using criteria for clarity, evidence, refutation, and listening Students leave with practiced speeches, debate materials, and a stronger ability to communicate with clarity and purpose.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to become more persuasive speakers, thoughtful listeners, and strategic participants in discussion. It fits interests in debate, law, government, business, leadership, journalism, or any field that values clear communication. Participants should be willing to speak in front of classmates, research an issue, collaborate with a team, and give and receive respectful feedback. No formal debate experience is required. Students who are ready to practice, revise, and engage with opposing views will benefit most.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Organize and deliver a persuasive speech for a defined audience • Construct and defend an evidence-based argument while addressing counterclaims • Evaluate a debate using criteria for clarity, evidence, refutation, and listening Students leave with practiced speeches, debate materials, and a stronger ability to communicate with clarity and purpose.

title: Advertising: Consumer Behavior & Campaign Strategy
subject: Business, Leadership & Entrepreneurship
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: Why does one advertisement connect while another gets ignored? Students explore advertising, marketing communications, and public relations across print, magazines, radio, television, social media, direct mail, and out-of-home media. They examine what a brand represents and how channel, message, and audience work together. Each class pairs concepts with a cr
description_full: Why does one advertisement connect while another gets ignored? Students explore advertising, marketing communications, and public relations across print, magazines, radio, television, social media, direct mail, and out-of-home media. They examine what a brand represents and how channel, message, and audience work together. Each class pairs concepts with a creative challenge. Teams respond to a brief by developing an advertisement in the medium under study, then explain how their idea fits the audience and objective. Discussions of challenger brands, celebrity endorsements, campaigns, and public relations show how communication choices can build attention, shape perception, or create risk. Quizzes reinforce vocabulary and strategy from previous sessions, while repeated team work builds speed and confidence. By comparing formats and creating across channels, students learn that an effective campaign requires more than a clever line. It needs a clear purpose, a specific audience, and execution suited to the way people encounter the message. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Define advertising, marketing communications, public relations, and brand strategy • Interpret a creative brief for a specific audience and objective • Develop print and magazine advertising concepts in teams • Adapt messages for direct mail and out-of-home formats • Create ideas for radio, television, and social media • Present creative choices and respond to peer feedback

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how audience, objective, brand, and medium shape an advertisement • Develop an advertising concept that responds to a creative brief • Compare communication formats and justify channel-specific creative choices Students leave with a set of cross-channel advertising concepts and a stronger foundation in strategic communications.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in advertising, brands, media, storytelling, consumer behavior, or public relations. It suits students who want to pair creative ideas with the strategy behind why a message works. Participants should be ready to discuss examples, work in teams, respond to briefs, present concepts, and learn through frequent quizzes and creative challenges. No specialized design software or prior advertising coursework is required. Curiosity about media and willingness to explain creative choices are strong indicators of fit.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how audience, objective, brand, and medium shape an advertisement • Develop an advertising concept that responds to a creative brief • Compare communication formats and justify channel-specific creative choices Students leave with a set of cross-channel advertising concepts and a stronger foundation in strategic communications.

description_short: What turns an idea into a business people can understand and support? description_full: What turns an idea into a business people can understand and support? Students examine the qualities of entrepreneurs, debate whether successful founders are born or made, and study the origin stories behind startups and iconic brands. Each discussion leads into a learning lab where they test the concept for themselves. Students create a graphic startup blueprint, use art and music to shape a business vision, and evaluate case studies about measured risk. They build a rubric for future risk decisions, explore failure and resiliency through a game, and create visual media for a dream startup using software tools. A course audio-podcast activity and final business presentation give them practice organizing ideas for an audience. The work develops a practical view of entrepreneurship without asking students to have their future figured out. They learn to explain a vision, consider evidence, respond to questions, and see how passion, innovation, risk, and resilience affect a startup. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Debate whether successful entrepreneurs are born or made • Research and record a startup founder for a course audio podcast • Create a graphic blueprint showing how a startup works • Shape and articulate a business vision through art and music • Evaluate risk cases and build a decision-making rubric • Create visual media and present a dream startup idea

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how vision, innovation, risk, and resilience influence a startup • Evaluate an entrepreneurial decision using evidence and a risk rubric • Organize and present a clear business idea for an audience Students will leave with a startup blueprint, visual media, and a business presentation, plus a clearer sense of which parts of entrepreneurship they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about how ideas become businesses. description_full: What turns an idea into a business people can understand and support? Students examine the qualities of entrepreneurs, debate whether successful founders are born or made, and study the origin stories behind startups and iconic brands. Each discussion leads into a learning lab where they test the concept for themselves. Students create a graphic startup blueprint, use art and music to shape a business vision, and evaluate case studies about measured risk. They build a rubric for future risk decisions, explore failure and resiliency through a game, and create visual media for a dream startup using software tools. A course audio-podcast activity and final business presentation give them practice organizing ideas for an audience. The work develops a practical view of entrepreneurship without asking students to have their future figured out. They learn to explain a vision, consider evidence, respond to questions, and see how passion, innovation, risk, and resilience affect a startup. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

description_full: What turns an interesting idea into a venture worth pursuing? Students enter a fast-moving startup studio and begin with opportunity recognition. In small teams, they identify a real problem, define the customer affected by it, and refine a concept through research, discussion, and feedback. The venture takes shape through the five Ps of business: product, price, promotion, place, and people. Students create a value proposition and logo, practice a speed pitch, explore marketing and sales, and consider how relationships, negotiation, culture, and international markets can affect execution. A simple financial snapshot asks teams to estimate startup costs, pricing, revenue, and feasibility. Teams also compare basic legal and business structures before preparing a one-page business summary and pitch deck. Each student speaks during the final presentation, explaining the problem, customer, solution, business logic, and changes made after feedback. The result is a practical introduction to iteration, teamwork, and the discipline behind entrepreneurial storytelling. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Identify a customer problem or market opportunity • Develop a value proposition and refine a business concept • Map product, price, promotion, place, and people • Create a logo, speed pitch, and one-page business summary • Estimate startup costs, pricing, revenue, and feasibility • Build and deliver a collaborative investor-style pitch

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Define a customer problem and develop a focused value proposition • Evaluate a venture using marketing, financial, and organizational considerations • Present and defend a refined business concept with a team Students leave with a pitch deck, business one-pager, financial snapshot, and experience turning feedback into a stronger venture.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to build ideas, solve problems, or understand how startups move from concept to pitch. It fits interests in entrepreneurship, business, design, technology, marketing, finance, or social innovation. Participants should be ready to collaborate intensively, make assumptions visible, use basic spreadsheets and presentation tools, and speak during a final pitch. Students who are comfortable testing an idea, hearing feedback, and revising quickly will gain the most.

description_short: How does the American legal system turn broad principles into decisions? description_full: How does the American legal system turn broad principles into decisions? Students examine the rule of law, justice, the Constitution, and the roles of the legislative, executive, and judicial branches. Landmark cases and current legal issues help them see how statutes, regulations, precedent, and constitutional rights shape everyday life. The course treats law as a practice, not only a body of facts. Students learn to brief a case by identifying the issue, relevant facts, reasoning, and decision. Small-group activities ask them to argue constitutional questions, compare civil and criminal matters, and follow a case through pleading, discovery, pretrial, trial, and post-trial stages. Legal vocabulary becomes useful through advocacy exercises. Students practice research, negotiation, cross-examination, and simulated trial work while considering the responsibilities of different legal professionals. Discussion emphasizes precise reasoning, supportable claims, and the ability to understand more than one side of a dispute. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Map the three branches of government and their legal roles • Analyze constitutional rights through a structured amendment argument • Brief a case by identifying issue, facts, reasoning, and decision • Compare civil and criminal cases and sources of law • Trace pleading, discovery, trial, and post-trial procedure • Practice negotiation, questioning, and simulated legal advocacy

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain core structures and sources within the American legal system • Brief a legal case and analyze competing arguments • Apply legal reasoning and advocacy skills in a simulated proceeding Students leave with case briefs, advocacy practice, and a clearer understanding of legal careers and the reasoning behind legal decisions.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in law, government, justice, policy, debate, or legal careers. It fits students who enjoy close reading, structured argument, and examining how rules apply to complicated facts. Participants should be ready to discuss contested issues respectfully, read cases, collaborate, and speak during simulations. Students who are willing to revise an argument when the facts or governing rule change will be especially well suited.

price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: Healthcare is a system of interconnected professions, not a single career track. Students compare clinical roles such as physicians, physician associates, nurses, and dentists with research, administration, policy, pharmaceutical, and health-technology pathways. For each, they examine daily responsibilities, working relationships, qualifications, and long-te
description_full: Healthcare is a system of interconnected professions, not a single career track. Students compare clinical roles such as physicians, physician associates, nurses, and dentists with research, administration, policy, pharmaceutical, and health-technology pathways. For each, they examine daily responsibilities, working relationships, qualifications, and long-term career outlook. The course follows the training behind the title. Students trace undergraduate, graduate, and professional steps, then consider how research advances medicine and how administrators and policy professionals shape care at scale. Discussions, projects, possible guest lectures, and videos connect formal pathways with the choices students can begin making in high school and college. Each student develops a personal career pathway project. Guided planning asks them to identify a profession of interest, relevant majors, education and training, volunteering or internship possibilities, and the strengths they want to build. A capstone presentation turns that research into a realistic next-step plan rather than a premature commitment. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Map the healthcare ecosystem and compare professional roles • Trace education and training for physicians, nurses, and physician associates • Explore dentistry, biomedical research, administration, policy, and health technology • Compare daily responsibilities and long-term career outlooks • Research majors, volunteering, internships, and preparation options • Create and present a personal healthcare career pathway

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare clinical, research, and administrative healthcare careers • Explain the education, qualifications, and responsibilities of a selected profession • Develop a researched personal action plan for continued healthcare exploration Students leave with a completed career pathway project and clearer next steps for exploring the diverse world of healthcare.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are considering medicine or want to understand the wider healthcare industry before choosing a direction. It fits interests in patient care, research, nursing, dentistry, policy, administration, pharmaceuticals, or health technology. Participants should be ready to research training pathways, ask questions, compare options, and reflect on their own interests and strengths. No clinical experience is required. Students who want an informed view of healthcare careers, including paths beyond becoming a physician, will benefit most.

subject: Humanities

description_short: What makes a college essay memorable when admissions readers already know a student’s grades and activities? Students learn how personal statements and supplemental essays can reveal character, perspective, growth, and goals. description_full: What makes a college essay memorable when admissions readers already know a student’s grades and activities? Students learn how personal statements and supplemental essays can reveal character, perspective, growth, and goals. Guided brainstorming helps them identify meaningful moments, mentors, challenges, identities, and experiences worth developing into an authentic story. The workshop moves from idea generation to deliberate craft. Students practice showing instead of telling, add sensory detail, adapt ideas to different prompts, and organize an essay with a clear structure. Sample essays, hook activities, outlines, scene writing, and peer read-alouds help them test openings, strengthen reflection, and make their voice sound natural rather than generic. Revision turns an early draft into a focused application essay. Students examine tone, sentence flow, verb tense, punctuation, fragments, run-ons, and other mechanics that affect clarity. Peer review, “So What?” checks, grammar activities, self-editing, and a final checklist help them refine meaning as well as correctness. By the end, each student completes a polished draft that stays within expected limits and represents their own experience. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities

description_full: What makes a college essay memorable when admissions readers already know a student’s grades and activities? Students learn how personal statements and supplemental essays can reveal character, perspective, growth, and goals. Guided brainstorming helps them identify meaningful moments, mentors, challenges, identities, and experiences worth developing into an authentic story. Students practice showing instead of telling, add sensory detail, adapt ideas to different prompts, and organize an essay with a clear structure. Sample essays, hook activities, outlines, scene writing, and peer read-alouds help them test openings, strengthen reflection, and make their voice sound natural rather than generic. Revision turns an early draft into a focused application essay. Students examine tone, sentence flow, verb tense, punctuation, fragments, run-ons, and other mechanics that affect clarity. Peer review, “So What?” checks, grammar activities, self-editing, and a final checklist help them refine meaning as well as correctness. By the end, each student completes a polished draft that stays within expected limits and represents their own experience. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. description_full: How does a college athlete become a credible brand? Students examine the business and media ecosystem of college sports, then study how name, image, and likeness has changed the relationship among athletes, schools, audiences, and commercial partners. Cases and discussion connect opportunity with legal and ethical responsibilities. The course moves from the landscape to personal brand architecture. Students define a story, values, audience, and point of difference, then plan content across social platforms. They analyze what brands look for in a partner, how sponsorship fit affects credibility, and why engagement strategy must serve more than follower growth. A Personal NIL Brand Pitch brings the work together. Each student develops a brand position, audience profile, content strategy, and potential partner fit, then presents the rationale with clarity and confidence. The project treats the athlete as both creator and decision-maker, emphasizing consistency, judgment, and responsible representation. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

description_full: Why do prices rise, recessions spread, or markets react to unexpected news? Students use those questions to build an introduction to economic thinking and the U.S. economy. They examine supply and demand, inflation, market fluctuations, and the choices consumers and businesses make when resources and information are limited. The course connects microeconomics with larger institutions and policy. Students consider how stock markets, consumer behavior, and different economic systems affect growth and opportunity. They also study how government and central institutions respond to changing conditions, weighing the intended effects and possible tradeoffs of policy choices. Global interdependence adds another layer. Discussions and activities explore trade, international finance, jobs, resources, and the way external shocks can travel across borders. Students practice applying concepts to current and historical examples, explaining not only what changed but also which incentives, institutions, and relationships help account for the outcome. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Model how supply and demand affect prices and market behavior • Compare economic systems and the incentives they create • Examine inflation, recession, and consumer responses • Analyze government policy tools and their possible tradeoffs • Trace how trade and finance connect national economies • Apply economic concepts to an external shock or market change

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain core economic concepts using relevant real-world examples • Analyze how policy, institutions, and consumer behavior influence markets • Evaluate an economic development by identifying incentives, tradeoffs, and global connections Students leave with applied economic analyses and a clearer framework for interpreting markets, policy, and global change.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are curious about prices, markets, government policy, business decisions, or global events. It fits interests in economics, finance, politics, international relations, data, or public policy. Participants should be ready to discuss competing explanations, work with basic economic relationships, and connect concepts to current and historical examples. Students who enjoy asking why outcomes change and considering tradeoffs will be well matched.

description_full: How do speakers turn an idea into a message people can follow? Students learn key concepts in public speaking and oratory communication while practicing speech making in a supportive setting. They examine topic selection, organization, speech writing, argument, and the relationship between a speaker and an audience. Guided practice helps students connect words with delivery. They work on verbal and nonverbal communication, prepare prompts, and consider how technology can support a presentation. Discussion and short exercises ask them to think before speaking, build knowledge about a topic, and choose an approach that fits the purpose. A persuasive speaking assignment brings the skills together. Students select an issue, organize a position, support it, and present to an audience. Feedback and reflection help them improve clarity and confidence while recognizing that effective speaking is interactive: good speakers also watch, listen, and adjust. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.body: • Select a focused topic for a speech • Organize ideas into a clear beginning, middle, and conclusion • Develop reasons and support for a persuasive claim • Practice verbal and nonverbal delivery techniques • Use presentation technology to support a message • Deliver a persuasive speech and respond to feedback

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Organize and deliver a speech for a specific purpose and audience • Support a persuasive claim with clear reasons and relevant information • Use verbal, nonverbal, and presentation choices to improve delivery Students leave with a completed persuasive speech and greater confidence communicating ideas to an audience.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and want to become more comfortable speaking in class, presenting ideas, or building persuasive arguments. It fits interests in debate, theater, leadership, writing, media, or civic discussion. Participants should be ready to choose topics, practice aloud, listen to classmates, and use feedback to revise. No previous public-speaking or debate experience is required. Students do not need to begin as confident speakers; a willingness to participate and improve is the most important fit.

subject: Law & Government

description_short: A crime scene cannot speak for itself. Students learn how investigators document, collect, preserve, and interpret evidence so that later conclusions can be tested. description_full: A crime scene cannot speak for itself. Students learn how investigators document, collect, preserve, and interpret evidence so that later conclusions can be tested. The course begins with forensic history, Locard’s exchange principle, scene safety, and the responsibilities involved in protecting evidence integrity. Hands-on work introduces crime-scene sketching, photography, fingerprint analysis, ballistics, blood-spatter patterns, trace evidence, and impression evidence. Students also examine simulated blood typing, time-of-death estimation using cooling, chromatography, toxicology, and the investigative questions connected to arson and explosives. Each technique requires careful observation and accurate recording. Evidence only becomes useful when the process is defensible. Students practice chain-of-custody thinking, compare what different evidence types can and cannot show, and bring findings together into a case strategy. The emphasis is on scientific reasoning, documentation, and measured conclusions rather than dramatic certainty. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Document a scene through notes, diagrams, sketches, and photography • Collect and preserve evidence while maintaining chain of custody • Compare fingerprints, impressions, and trace evidence • Examine ballistics and blood-spatter pattern evidence • Use chromatography and simulated blood typing in analysis • Estimate time of death and integrate findings into a case strategy

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Document and preserve a simulated crime scene using forensic procedures • Analyze multiple evidence types and explain what each finding supports • Construct a case interpretation that distinguishes observations, inferences, and limitations Students leave with forensic documentation, laboratory analyses, and a stronger understanding of evidence integrity and case reconstruction.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in forensic science, criminal justice, biology, chemistry, investigation, or law. It suits students who enjoy careful observation and using several types of evidence to answer a larger question. Participants should be ready to follow safety procedures, record details precisely, work with classmates, and explain conclusions without overstating certainty. Patience, curiosity, and respect for evidence are especially important.

description_full: How can a small clue change an investigation? Students explore how scientific methods help people examine a crime scene and test possible explanations. The course emphasizes observation, evidence collection, documentation, and the difference between what a clue shows and what an investigator thinks it might mean. Hands-on activities introduce trace evidence, fingerprints, handwriting, and photographic evidence. Students compare samples, record patterns, and use real-world case studies to see how several pieces of information can support or challenge a theory. Laboratory-style work builds care, patience, and attention to procedure. As the course progresses, students combine findings to solve age-appropriate investigative problems. Discussion and reflection help them explain their reasoning, listen to alternative interpretations, and revise a conclusion when new evidence appears. The focus is not guessing the answer first. It is building a case that another person can follow. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

description_full: How can a small clue change an investigation? Students explore how scientific methods help people examine a crime scene and test possible explanations. The course emphasizes observation, evidence collection, documentation, and the difference between what a clue shows and what an investigator thinks it might mean. Hands-on activities introduce trace evidence, fingerprints, handwriting, and photographic evidence. Students compare samples, record patterns, and use real-world case studies to see how several pieces of information can support or challenge a theory. Laboratory-style work builds care, patience, and attention to procedure. As the course progresses, students combine findings to solve age-appropriate investigative problems. Discussion and reflection help them explain their reasoning, listen to alternative interpretations, and revise a conclusion when new evidence appears. The focus is not guessing the answer first. It is building a case that another person can follow. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. description_full: How can organizations create value while responding to global challenges? Students use the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals as a framework for examining leadership, business, and social impact. Case studies, discussions, guest speakers, and hands-on exercises show how companies and nonprofits connect strategy with needs in communities around the world. Students study the 17 goals, select issues that matter to them, and translate research into visual communication. An infographic exercise asks them to identify meaningful data and explain why a goal deserves attention. They then examine executive summaries, mission, market context, operations, funding, and the choices leaders make when resources and priorities compete. The course culminates in a sustainable business or nonprofit plan. Students define the problem, propose a solution, outline implementation, and build five-year financial projections showing revenue, expenses, cash flow, and potential investor returns. Presentations require them to connect impact goals with a practical plan and respond to questions about feasibility and leadership. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.body: • Connect the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals to business challenges • Research one global goal and create a data-based infographic • Analyze how organizations address social and environmental needs • Draft an executive summary and operating approach • Build five-year revenue, expense, and cash-flow projections • Present a sustainable business or nonprofit plan

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how selected Sustainable Development Goals relate to organizational strategy • Develop a practical venture plan with impact and financial considerations • Present and defend a sustainable business or nonprofit proposal Students leave with an infographic, a developed venture plan, and experience connecting global purpose with practical leadership decisions.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in leadership, global issues, entrepreneurship, sustainability, business, or nonprofit work. It fits students who want to turn concern about a problem into a researched and structured response. Participants should be ready to discuss complex issues, work with data, collaborate on planning, use basic presentation and spreadsheet tools, and explain financial assumptions. Curiosity about how institutions create change will help students thrive.

Discussion emphasizes critical understanding, respectful disagreement, and the relationship between publi
description_full: Who has the authority to act when Americans disagree about rights, policy, or public priorities? Students approach that question by examining the constitutional structure of the federal government and connecting it to current domestic and foreign issues. Discussion emphasizes critical understanding, respectful disagreement, and the relationship between public events and course concepts. The course moves through the legislative, executive, and judicial branches, including congressional lawmaking, presidential power, federal agencies, checks and balances, and the Supreme Court. Students analyze major cases and explore the Bill of Rights through an assigned-amendment presentation. They also consider barriers to civic participation and the responsibilities of active citizens in a democratic society. A civic-engagement presentation asks each student to identify something they would like to change or improve. Classmates then evaluate whether the legislative, executive, or judicial branch has the constitutional or practical authority to address it. Visits to the United States Capitol and a local courthouse let students question Senate staff and a judge, connecting classroom analysis to institutions in action. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Examine the powers and limits of Congress, the presidency, and the federal courts • Analyze checks and balances and significant Supreme Court cases • Investigate freedoms protected by the Bill of Rights • Present the importance of an assigned constitutional amendment • Debate current issues through respectful, evidence-based civil discourse • Develop a civic-engagement presentation about a desired change • Visit the United States Capitol and a local courthouse

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how constitutional powers and checks shape the three federal branches • Analyze civil liberties and current issues using course evidence • Present a realistic civic action and identify which institutions can address it Students leave with completed civic presentations, direct exposure to government institutions, stronger analysis and discussion skills, and greater clarity about continued study, a possible major, or a pathway in law, policy, government, or civic work.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in American government, constitutional law, current events, civil liberties, public policy, or civic participation. It suits students who want to understand how institutions work and how people can engage them. Participants should be ready to discuss potentially controversial topics respectfully, connect news and observations to course material, prepare short presentations, and ask thoughtful questions during off-site visits. No particular political viewpoint is expected, and students are not required to disclose personal positions or experiences. Curiosity, preparation, and a willingness to examine competing interpretations will help students contribute to a serious and constructive classroom.

title: International Relations: Geopolitics & Diplomacy
subject: Law & Government
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: Why do states cooperate in some moments and compete in others? Students are introduced to nations as actors in an international system and to the forces shaping their choices. Core concepts include anarchy, power, authority, levels of analysis, balance of power, and the theories used to explain conflict and cooperation. Historical and current cases give the
description_full: Why do states cooperate in some moments and compete in others? Students are introduced to nations as actors in an international system and to the forces shaping their choices. Core concepts include anarchy, power, authority, levels of analysis, balance of power, and the theories used to explain conflict and cooperation. Historical and current cases give the concepts weight. Students consider nuclear deterrence, the World Wars, the Cold War, the Russian invasion of Ukraine, conflict involving the United States, Israel, and Iran, international organizations, and global environmental issues. Readings and discussion ask them to compare explanations rather than treat one account as complete. A foreign-policy discussion assignment turns analysis into advocacy. Working in groups or individually, students represent a political actor, use data to construct a coherent position, and present that argument persuasively. Final assessment and reflection ask them to connect concepts, evidence, and communication while recognizing the interests and constraints different actors face. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Apply levels of analysis to an international event • Compare theories of conflict, power, and cooperation • Examine balance of power and nuclear deterrence • Analyze the role of international organizations • Investigate a global environmental or security issue • Build and present a data-supported foreign-policy position

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Use international-relations concepts to explain state behavior • Compare competing interpretations of a global conflict or policy problem • Construct and defend a coherent foreign-policy argument using evidence Students leave with a completed policy discussion project and a stronger framework for interpreting global events and institutions.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and follow world events or are interested in politics, history, diplomacy, conflict, environmental issues, or international organizations. It suits students who want analytical tools for understanding why global actors make different choices. Participants should be ready to read, discuss contested events, work with classmates, use data, and represent a perspective they may not personally hold. Respectful debate and willingness to compare explanations are essential.
