description_full: Who helps a patient recover, prevent illness, or understand a diagnosis? Students explore medicine through the many professionals who contribute to patient care and community health. Clinical medicine, emergency care, biomedical research, public health, genetics, healthcare administration, ethics, and career pathways provide a broad view of the field. Interactive activities make the healthcare system easier to see. In a healthcare team challenge, students receive patient scenarios such as a broken arm, asthma attack, or diabetes diagnosis, then identify the physicians, nurses, pharmacists, therapists, assistants, and other professionals involved. Case studies and discussions ask them to consider how teams share information and make patient-centered decisions. The course culminates in a Healthcare Career Project. Students investigate one profession, explain its role and training, and connect it to their interests and strengths. Simulations, guest speakers when available, and hands-on projects help students move from a general interest in medicine to specific questions they can continue exploring. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.body: • Build a healthcare team map for a patient scenario • Compare clinical, research, public health, and administrative roles • Discuss emergency care, genetics, and medical ethics • Apply problem-solving to age-appropriate healthcare cases • Investigate the education and work of one healthcare profession • Create and present a Healthcare Career Project

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Describe how healthcare professionals collaborate in patient-centered care • Compare several clinical, research, and public health careers • Research and present the role and pathway of a selected profession Students leave with a completed career project and a clearer picture of how their interests might connect to healthcare.

title: Mock Trial: Courtroom Strategy & Advocacy
subject: Law & Government
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: On Georgetown University’s campus in Washington, D.C., students explore courtroom strategy in a city closely associated with law, policy, and public institutions. A trial is a coordinated process in which every role sees the case differently. Students examine the responsibilities of attorneys, defendants, witnesses, judges, and jurors, then study how legal t
description_full: On Georgetown University’s campus in Washington, D.C., students explore courtroom strategy in a city closely associated with law, policy, and public institutions. A trial is a coordinated process in which every role sees the case differently. Students examine the responsibilities of attorneys, defendants, witnesses, judges, and jurors, then study how legal teams prepare a hypothetical case. Jury selection and voir dire introduce the questions advocates use to understand a potential jury. Working in teams from a mock-trial packet, students develop opening and closing statements, prepare direct and cross-examination questions, and learn when evidence may be introduced or challenged. Practice sessions require them to make objections, respond to an opponent, and revise strategy as the case takes shape. The culminating mock trial puts preparation into motion. Students present arguments, question witnesses, manage exhibits, and respond in real time while maintaining courtroom procedure. Reflection and feedback connect courtroom performance with the critical thinking, problem-solving, teamwork, and public speaking skills that effective advocacy requires. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities

description_full: On Georgetown University’s campus in Washington, D.C., students explore courtroom strategy in a city closely associated with law, policy, and public institutions. A trial is a coordinated process in which every role sees the case differently. Students examine the responsibilities of attorneys, defendants, witnesses, judges, and jurors, then study how legal teams prepare a hypothetical case. Jury selection and voir dire introduce the questions advocates use to understand a potential jury. Working in teams from a mock-trial packet, students develop opening and closing statements, prepare direct and cross-examination questions, and learn when evidence may be introduced or challenged. Practice sessions require them to make objections, respond to an opponent, and revise strategy as the case takes shape. The culminating mock trial puts preparation into motion. Students present arguments, question witnesses, manage exhibits, and respond in real time while maintaining courtroom procedure. Reflection and feedback connect courtroom performance with the critical thinking, problem-solving, teamwork, and public speaking skills that effective advocacy requires. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

description_full: How can money today support a goal years from now? Students build an accessible introduction to finance, investment management, and capital markets. They examine saving, interest rates, and the power of compounding before comparing how stocks, bonds, funds, and cryptocurrency differ in risk, return, volatility, and liquidity. The course turns concepts into decisions. Students define financial goals and time horizons, explore personal risk tolerance, and study why diversification matters. Research and simulation activities ask them to interpret company or economic news, distinguish expectations from outcomes, and recognize common behavioral pitfalls such as acting from fear or excitement. By the end of the course, students design a personal investment portfolio. Their choices must fit a stated goal, time horizon, risk and reward tolerance, and diversification plan. The emphasis is on responsible decision-making, patience, and explaining a strategy, not on promising a particular return. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Calculate how compounding affects savings over time • Compare stocks, bonds, funds, and cryptocurrency • Assess personal goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance • Research how company and economic news may affect investments • Identify behavioral pitfalls in investment decisions • Design and explain a diversified personal portfolio

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain compounding, risk and return, volatility, liquidity, and diversification • Compare common investment types in relation to a financial goal • Construct a diversified portfolio aligned with time horizon and risk tolerance Students leave with a completed personal portfolio plan and a stronger foundation for responsible saving and investing decisions.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and want to understand saving, investing, markets, or how financial goals shape decisions. It fits students who enjoy working with numbers and asking why an investment may rise, fall, or suit one person better than another. Participants should be ready to compare options, conduct basic research, join simulations, and explain their portfolio choices. No previous finance or economics experience is required. Patience, curiosity, and a willingness to think beyond short-term headlines will support success.

description_short: Why do people think, learn, feel, and behave as they do? Students survey major principles and perspectives in psychology, beginning with the field’s history and scientific foundations. They compare theoretical frameworks and learn how psychologists turn questions about behavior into research that can be observed, measured, and critiqued. The course examines
description_full: Why do people think, learn, feel, and behave as they do? Students survey major principles and perspectives in psychology, beginning with the field’s history and scientific foundations. They compare theoretical frameworks and learn how psychologists turn questions about behavior into research that can be observed, measured, and critiqued. The course examines biological bases of behavior from neural and chemical processes to the central and peripheral nervous systems. Students then connect biology with development, learning, motivation, emotion, memory, cognition, personality, and social interaction. Examples and activities ask them to distinguish a plausible explanation from a claim supported by research. Research methods provide a thread across the topics. Students compare observational, correlational, experimental, and quasi-experimental designs, considering the strengths and limitations of each. By analyzing studies and theories, they practice asking what the evidence supports, what remains uncertain, and how psychological knowledge can be applied responsibly. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare historical and current perspectives in psychology • Examine neural, physiological, and chemical bases of behavior • Analyze learning, motivation, emotion, memory, and cognition • Explore development, personality, and social interaction • Compare observational, correlational, experimental, and quasi-experimental methods • Critique psychological studies for strengths, limits, and conclusions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Differentiate major psychological perspectives and fields of study • Compare research methods and evaluate the limits of a study • Explain behavior using biological, cognitive, developmental, and social evidence Students leave with research critiques and a stronger scientific framework for interpreting human behavior and mental processes.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in psychology, neuroscience, human development, behavior, mental health, or research. It suits students who want to understand both major topics and how psychologists build reliable knowledge. Participants should be ready to discuss studies, compare theories, analyze evidence, and question conclusions thoughtfully. Students who are curious about people and willing to test intuition against research will be a strong fit. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Differentiate major psychological perspectives and fields of study • Compare research methods and evaluate the limits of a study • Explain behavior using biological, cognitive, developmental, and social evidence Students leave with research critiques and a stronger scientific framework for interpreting human behavior and mental processes.

title: Public Health: Protecting Communities & Preventing Disease
raw_title: Public Health: Protecting Communities & Preventing Disease
subject: Medicine & Health Sciences
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How can a community prevent illness before someone reaches a clinic? Students explore public health at the intersection of medicine, policy, behavior, and the conditions that shape population health. Historical and modern cases introduce the field’s purpose, major institutions, and the difference between treating an individual and improving outcomes across g
description_full: How can a community prevent illness before someone reaches a clinic? Students explore public health at the intersection of medicine, policy, behavior, and the conditions that shape population health. Historical and modern cases introduce the field’s purpose, major institutions, and the difference between treating an individual and improving outcomes across groups. The course examines pandemics and other public health challenges, including the Spanish flu, sickle cell anemia, and COVID-19. Students connect epidemiology, sanitation, vaccines, immunology, prevention, and intervention to the way health problems are measured and addressed. They also evaluate health messaging and marketing materials for audience, clarity, credibility, and likely effect. A final project asks students to apply a public health perspective to a real-world problem. They identify an affected population, analyze contributing factors, and propose strategies that may improve health. The project emphasizes evidence, feasible prevention or intervention, and communication that respects the people a solution is meant to serve. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Define public health and distinguish population from individual care • Examine historical and modern health crises • Connect epidemiology, sanitation, vaccines, and immunology • Identify prevention and intervention strategies • Evaluate health messages for accuracy and audience fit • Design and present a population-focused public health response

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how public health addresses health at the population level • Evaluate prevention strategies and health communication using evidence • Develop a feasible intervention proposal for a defined public health problem Students leave with a completed intervention proposal and a stronger framework for understanding health through medicine, policy, and society.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in health, medicine, biology, policy, equity, communication, or global issues. It fits students who want to understand why communities experience different health outcomes and how prevention can work at scale. Participants should be ready to discuss sensitive health topics respectfully, analyze cases and messages, work with classmates, and propose an evidence-informed solution. Curiosity about both science and social systems is a strong fit.

description_full: Why do people remember some things, follow a group, or react differently in the same situation? Students explore foundational psychology through questions about thought, behavior, and social influence. They learn how psychologists develop theories and use research methods to study experiences that may feel familiar but are not always simple to explain. The course moves through neuroscience, learning and motivation, memory and cognition, social psychology, and health and well-being. Discussions and activities help students compare how the brain, past experience, goals, identity, and the surrounding situation may influence what a person notices or does. Students practice reading psychological claims carefully and connecting them to evidence. Rather than diagnosing themselves or others, they focus on concepts, research findings, and respectful discussion. By the end, they have a broader vocabulary for asking good questions about the mind and recognizing how context can shape behavior. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Explore how psychologists develop and test explanations • Examine basic links between the brain and behavior • Compare learning, motivation, memory, and cognition • Discuss how social situations and groups influence people • Connect psychological concepts to health and well-being • Evaluate an age-appropriate psychological claim using evidence

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Describe foundational psychological concepts related to mind and behavior • Explain how individual and social factors can influence an outcome • Evaluate a psychological claim by asking how it was studied Students leave with a stronger vocabulary for psychology and a more evidence-focused way to think about behavior and social influence.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend

description_full: Why do people remember some things, follow a group, or react differently in the same situation? Students explore foundational psychology through questions about thought, behavior, and social influence. They learn how psychologists develop theories and use research methods to study experiences that may feel familiar but are not always simple to explain. The course moves through neuroscience, learning and motivation, memory and cognition, social psychology, and health and well-being. Discussions and activities help students compare how the brain, past experience, goals, identity, and the surrounding situation may influence what a person notices or does. Students practice reading psychological claims carefully and connecting them to evidence. Rather than diagnosing themselves or others, they focus on concepts, research findings, and respectful discussion. By the end, they have a broader vocabulary for asking good questions about the mind and recognizing how context can shape behavior. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

description_full: How do culture, institutions, and relationships shape individual choices? Students use the sociological imagination to connect personal experiences with larger social patterns. Topics include culture, childhood development, family and social relationships, deviance, race relations, population, sexuality and gender, and large-scale social change. The course also introduces sociology as a research discipline. Students compare experiments, surveys, field research, content analysis, and other quantitative or qualitative approaches. They examine ethics, literature reviews, hypotheses, validity, and reliability, learning how the design of a study affects the conclusions it can support. Applied exercises move from critique to design. Students conduct a short content analysis and develop a simple field-research proposal or project. By connecting theory, method, and observation, they learn to ask sociological questions carefully and to examine social claims without reducing complex people or institutions to stereotypes. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Apply the sociological imagination to culture and institutions • Compare quantitative and qualitative research approaches • Identify ethical issues in social research • Formulate a testable hypothesis and select measures • Conduct a short content analysis • Design a simple field-research project

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how social structures and culture shape behavior and outcomes • Compare research methods for a defined sociological question • Design an ethical study with a testable hypothesis and appropriate evidence Students leave with a content analysis, a research design, and a stronger method for examining claims about society.

Participants should be ready to discuss complex topics respectfully, read research, compare methods, and question assumptions. Students who enjoy observing patterns and asking how evidence was gathered will be a strong fit. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

description_full: What makes a sports contract work for an athlete, team, league, or sponsor? Students begin by comparing amateur, professional, and international sports, then apply contract and tort law to sporting-event scenarios. NCAA eligibility, recruiting rules, and the transfer portal provide a second set of fact patterns where one decision can change what is permissible. The course then moves into NIL agreements, Title IX, collective bargaining, and alternative dispute resolution. Students evaluate pay-for-play and recruiting questions, examine what happens when labor negotiations stall, and practice negotiation, mediation, and arbitration through a sports-agent exercise. Antitrust law, the MLB exemption, representation and marketability, and conflicts of interest show how legal strategy shapes the business of sports. Students brief a case, compare endorsement, licensing, sponsorship, copyright, and trademark issues, and spot ethical questions involving gambling, doping, safety, and technology. The course culminates in a final exam. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. Students may request an official Georgetown University transcript. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Apply contract and tort law to sporting-event scenarios • Evaluate NCAA eligibility, recruiting, and transfer-portal fact patterns • Analyze NIL pay-for-play agreements and Title IX requirements • Practice negotiation, mediation, and arbitration in a sports-agent exercise • Brief a case and compare antitrust, endorsement, licensing, copyright, and trademark issues • Spot ethical questions involving gambling, doping, safety, and technology

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze how contracts, torts, labor rules, antitrust law, and intellectual property affect sports organizations • Evaluate NIL, NCAA recruiting, Title IX, and agent scenarios using relevant legal standards • Compare negotiation, mediation, arbitration, and collective bargaining as methods for resolving sports disputes Students will leave with a completed case brief, legal scenario analyses, sports-agent negotiation experience, and greater clarity about studying sports law or a related field.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to understand the rules behind athletes, teams, leagues, colleges, agents, and brands. It fits students interested in law, sports management, business, communications, public policy, college athletics, or the business of professional sports. Participants should be ready to read fact patterns, take notes, discuss evolving legal questions, collaborate in small groups, practice negotiations, and prepare for a final exam. Students who enjoy weighing competing interests and supporting a position with evidence will find several ways to contribute. The course can fit avid sports followers as well as students primarily curious about how law shapes a major industry.

description_full: What happens behind the scenes before a team takes the field? Students explore the business side of sports, including how teams are organized, how players are evaluated, how contracts work, and how games become global events and community platforms. They compare the responsibilities of owners, general managers, coaches, agents, and other front-office roles. Each class combines short lessons with interactive decisions. Students use data in player-evaluation challenges, practice mock drafts and negotiations, examine contracts and trademarks, and explore sponsorships and name, image, and likeness. Design work around stadiums, safety, and fan experience shows how game-day operations combine planning with service. Press-conference activities ask students to explain and defend their choices. Team projects also examine international growth, brand partnerships, and the social responsibilities of sports organizations. The course connects competition on the field with money, law, marketing, analytics, operations, and community impact. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Map the roles in a professional sports front office • Use data to compare players and make roster decisions • Practice a mock draft and contract negotiation • Explore sports law, rights, trademarks, and NIL • Design elements of a safe, engaging game-day experience • Defend team decisions in a simulated press conference

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how major front-office roles contribute to a sports organization • Use basic evidence to support a player, contract, or operations decision • Present and defend a sports-management recommendation Students leave with completed front-office challenges and a clearer understanding of the careers and decisions behind organized sports.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and love sports and want to understand the business beyond the scoreboard. It fits interests in management, statistics, law, marketing, events, media, or team leadership. Participants should be ready to collaborate, make decisions from evidence, negotiate respectfully, design solutions, and answer questions in press-conference activities. No playing experience or prior business coursework is required. Curiosity about how teams operate is the strongest prerequisite. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

description_short: What makes countries cooperate, and what pushes them into conflict? Students begin by examining nations as actors in an international system and learning how power, security, institutions, and identity can shape their choices. They compare major perspectives such as realism, liberalism, and constructivism, then use those ideas to make sense of alliances, nuc
description_full: What makes countries cooperate, and what pushes them into conflict? Students begin by examining nations as actors in an international system and learning how power, security, institutions, and identity can shape their choices. They compare major perspectives such as realism, liberalism, and constructivism, then use those ideas to make sense of alliances, nuclear deterrence, diplomacy, and international law. Historical and contemporary examples help students connect theory to events with global consequences. Through readings, case analysis, multimedia, and discussion, they consider the Cold War, international organizations, environmental challenges, and questions of race, gender, and legitimacy in world politics. The goal is not to memorize one explanation, but to see how different frameworks can lead to different conclusions. For the culminating foreign policy discussion, students represent a political actor, gather evidence, and work in teams to recommend a government response to an international problem. They organize their reasoning in a foreign policy brief and present a persuasive argument to the class. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare realism, liberalism, and constructivism as explanations of world events • Examine alliances, nuclear deterrence, diplomacy, and international organizations • Analyze historical and contemporary issues through readings, cases, and discussion • Represent a political actor in a team foreign policy discussion • Gather evidence and develop a response to an international problem • Present and defend a persuasive foreign policy brief

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare major international-relations theories and apply them to global events • Analyze how power, institutions, identity, and competing interests shape foreign policy • Develop and present an evidence-based response to an international problem Students will leave with a completed foreign policy brief, experience presenting a team argument, and a clearer sense of which global issues they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about world events, diplomacy, politics, conflict, or how countries work together. It is a strong fit for students who enjoy asking why governments make certain choices and considering how the same issue may look from several perspectives. Students should be ready to read, discuss ideas, work with a team, and support an argument with evidence. Curiosity and a willingness to listen, question assumptions, and revise an idea are more important than already having firm opinions about international affairs.

description_full: Good engineering research begins before anything is built. It starts with a question that is specific enough to investigate and important enough to pursue. Students learn how researchers move from a broad interest to a defensible question, a workable method, and a clear plan for gathering evidence. Through literature analysis, research-design exercises, case studies, and proposal workshops, students compare qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods. They practice evaluating source quality, considering ethics, defining variables, and selecting methods that fit an engineering problem. Feedback from peers and the instructor helps students narrow the scope of their ideas and strengthen the logic behind each decision. This hybrid academy combines an on-campus experience with Polygence’s Core Research Program. During the campus program, each student develops an engineering research proposal, abstract, and professional scientific poster, then presents the work in a symposium-style setting. Afterward, students join a virtual cohort and are matched 1:1 with a Polygence research mentor in their field of interest. Across 10 virtual sessions, the mentor helps each student continue the project at an individual pace toward a research paper, symposium presentation, podcast, or another appropriate final format. description_full: How can a robot sense its environment and act on a real need? Students trace the history of robotics from early mechanisms to industrial systems, soft robotics, autonomous machines, and AI-driven automation. Examples from healthcare, manufacturing, architecture, space exploration, and disaster response show how design choices depend on the problem being solved. Hands-on work introduces circuitry, sensors, mechanical design, building, and programming. Students assemble and code robotic systems, experiment with an XRP robot, and explore soft-robotics fabrication. Guided practice and testing help them see how hardware, software, and physical constraints interact when a system does not behave as planned. For the capstone, teams identify a real-world problem, research stakeholders, write a focused problem statement, and propose an innovative robotic solution. They develop the design, consider function and constraints, and present how the robot could address the need. Industry speakers and visits, when available, add context from the Bay Area robotics ecosystem. This two-week full-day academy is part of Summer Discovery at UC Berkeley, held on the university’s campus. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. A supplemental course fee of $195 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Trace major milestones and emerging trends in robotics • Build and program an XRP robotic system • Connect circuitry and sensors to physical behavior • Experiment with mechanical design and soft robotics • Research stakeholders and define a real-world problem • Design and present an innovative robotic solution

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how mechanical, electronic, and computational elements form a robotic system • Build and program a robot to complete defined behaviors • Develop and defend a stakeholder-centered robotic solution Students leave with built robotic systems, code, and a capstone proposal connecting engineering choices to a real-world need.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in robotics, engineering, coding, design, automation, or applied problem-solving. It fits students who want to understand both how robots work and why particular systems are built. Participants should be ready to build, program, troubleshoot, collaborate, and present a team solution. No prior robotics experience is required. Persistence is important because testing and revision are expected parts of engineering work. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

description_full: A strong business idea starts with a problem worth solving. Students begin by looking for unmet needs, testing whether an idea creates real value and narrowing their thinking to one original venture concept. Using the NFTE curriculum, they organize the idea with a Lean Business Model Canvas. Market research helps them define a target customer, estimate demand and understand buying patterns. Competitive analysis and a SWOT evaluation sharpen the value proposition, while branding and marketing workshops turn that strategy into a message customers can understand. Students then examine fixed and variable costs, pricing, revenue models and the point where a business can break even. They assemble their research and decisions into a professional pitch deck, practice answering questions and revise their work through peer and instructor feedback. The course culminates in a Fast Pitch Challenge evaluated with NFTE’s official rubric. Along the way, students consider how entrepreneurial choices affect customers and communities, adding responsibility and impact to the venture discussion. Students examine a major issue affecting communities in the Global South, identify root causes and gaps in existing solutions, and ask what a new venture could change responsibly. Startup teams compare traditional and social-enterprise models, study global venture cases, and develop a solution around the needs of a defined customer or stakeholder group. Their final proposal includes the issue, solution, business model, outreach and marketing plan, measures of impact, budget, and financing request. Peer feedback helps each group turn separate ideas into one cohesive case for action before a Demo Day presentation, where teams work within time limits and answer live questions. For the capstone, students design a case-based presentation focused on a chosen health profession. Each student develops and presents at least one case within a team format. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. Across the academy, students reflect on the strengths, knowledge, and next steps involved in exploring a brain-science health career. Their capstone brings that reflection into a practical plan, which they develop with structured work time and present to classmates and instructors. Repeated case discussions help them connect scientific detail with careful, humane communication across different clinical perspectives. This two-week full-day academy is part of Summer Discovery at UC Berkeley, held on the university’s campus. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Map neurotransmitters and connect neural pathways to clinical conditions • Examine brain anatomy through a guided laboratory activity • Conduct a patient interview and complete a mental status examination • Evaluate psychiatry cases in an ethics board simulation • Design multidisciplinary treatment plans for complex patient scenarios • Present a capstone plan for continued exploration of brain-science careers

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how neural mechanisms and clinical evidence inform mental-health assessment • Apply ethical and multidisciplinary reasoning to patient cases and treatment plans • Conduct and communicate a structured analysis of a psychiatric scenario Students will leave with clinical case work and a personal exploration plan, deeper neuroscience and communication skills, and greater clarity about continued study or careers in brain science and healthcare.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in the brain, mental health, medicine, or the decisions clinicians make when a case is complex. It can help students compare possible directions in psychiatry, neuroscience, psychology, public health, and related health fields. No clinical experience is expected. Students should be prepared to participate respectfully in role-play, case discussion, group planning, and presentations. The course addresses serious themes, including mental illness, trauma, eating disorders, and substance use. Students and families should consider the course’s mature subject matter when deciding whether the experience is a good fit.

description_full: ACT/SAT Success Studio is a specialized test-prep course delivered by ESM Prep as part of the program held on UCLA’s campus. description_full: How can a computer find patterns in data and use them to make a prediction? Students build Python fundamentals through guided notebooks, then connect code to machine-learning tasks in natural language processing, computer vision, healthcare, sustainability, and assistive technology. Projects make the machine-learning pipeline concrete. Students customize a chatbot, analyze real-world data, and explore a decision-tree model that predicts heart-disease risk. Additional examples may include crop-yield prediction, movie recommendations, autonomous vehicles, social robots, or tools for disaster relief. Ethical discussions ask who benefits, who may be excluded, and what can go wrong when data or design assumptions are weak. For the collaborative capstone, teams select a meaningful problem and develop an AI application or prototype. They define the goal, prepare or interpret data, test a model, evaluate limitations, and present both the technical approach and the intended social impact. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Build Python skills through guided coding notebooks • Customize a chatbot using natural-language concepts • Train and interpret a decision-tree model with health data • Explore AI applications in sustainability and assistive technology • Evaluate bias, privacy, accessibility, and model limitations • Develop and present a collaborative AI-for-good capstone

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Use Python fundamentals to complete guided data and AI tasks • Explain the basic machine-learning pipeline and evaluate a model’s limitations • Collaborate on an AI application that addresses a social-impact problem Students will leave with coded projects, experience interpreting real-world data, and a capstone presentation, along with a clearer sense of which areas of AI they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about coding, artificial intelligence, data, or how technology can address real problems. It is a strong fit for students who are willing to learn Python and work through coding challenges. Students should be ready to work through coding errors, collaborate on a project, discuss ethical questions, and explain what a model can and cannot do. A strong participant brings curiosity, patience, and a willingness to revise. The most important preparation is readiness to ask questions and take part.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Use Python fundamentals to complete guided data and AI tasks • Explain the basic machine-learning pipeline and evaluate a model’s limitations • Collaborate on an AI application that addresses a social-impact problem Students will leave with coded projects, experience interpreting real-world data, and a capstone presentation, along with a clearer sense of which areas of AI they may want to explore next.

subject: Medicine & Health Sciences
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: Two patients may share a symptom and still require different diagnoses. Students learn to look past a single clue, compare the full pattern and ask what evidence separates one psychological disorder from another. The course examines mood, anxiety, personality, psychotic, trauma-related, eating and neurocognitive disorders. Case studies challenge students to
description_full: Two patients may share a symptom and still require different diagnoses. Students learn to look past a single clue, compare the full pattern and ask what evidence separates one psychological disorder from another. The course examines mood, anxiety, personality, psychotic, trauma-related, eating and neurocognitive disorders. Case studies challenge students to apply DSM-5-TR criteria, while differential-diagnosis activities ask them to distinguish closely related conditions such as Bipolar I, Bipolar II and major depressive disorder. Students also compare psychodynamic, Adlerian, cognitive behavioral, narrative and Gestalt explanations of symptoms. A psychological-assessment role-play shows how clinicians gather and interpret information, including the limits and complexity of diagnosis. Students practice holding multiple hypotheses and revising a conclusion when new details change the case. That discipline matters throughout the capstone. For the capstone, each student selects a fictional or nonfictional character, studies the character’s history and symptoms, builds an evidence-supported diagnosis and presents the analysis in a paper or presentation. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare major categories of psychological disorders using DSM-5-TR criteria • Analyze hypothetical clients through individual and group case studies • Practice differential diagnosis between disorders with overlapping symptoms • Compare psychodynamic, Adlerian, cognitive behavioral, narrative and Gestalt viewpoints • Explore psychological assessment through a case-based role-play and inventory • Diagnose a selected character and present an evidence-supported capstone analysis

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Differentiate major psychological disorders using symptoms, history and diagnostic criteria • Compare how several psychological orientations explain symptoms and treatment • Construct and defend a case-based diagnosis using relevant evidence Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a diagnostic case capstone and greater clarity about studying psychology, mental health or a related clinical field.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in psychology, mental health, human behavior or clinical decision-making. It is especially relevant for students who want to move beyond introductory psychology and examine how professionals assess complex cases. Students should be ready to discuss sensitive topics respectfully, compare multiple explanations, read diagnostic criteria and support their conclusions with evidence. The class does not train students to diagnose people in their own lives; its cases and role-plays are structured academic exercises.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Differentiate major psychological disorders using symptoms, history and diagnostic criteria • Compare how several psychological orientations explain symptoms and treatment • Construct and defend a case-based diagnosis using relevant evidence Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a diagnostic case capstone and greater clarity about studying psychology, mental health or a related clinical field.

subject: Business, Leadership & Entrepreneurship
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: A logo may attract attention, but a campaign works only when the brand, audience, message and media support the same idea. Market research and audience decisions shape a market
description_full: A logo may attract attention, but a campaign works only when the brand, audience, message and media support the same idea. Students begin by examining the Four Ps of marketing and the reasons familiar brands are memorable. They then create a company, name its product and design an initial visual identity. Market research and audience decisions shape a marketing plan. Students develop messaging, slogans and jingles, choose media channels and build creative assets with tools such as Canva, PowerPoint or Google Slides. They study advertising techniques through real campaigns, then write and record a 30-second radio spot or storyboard a television commercial. Public relations adds another layer. Students write a press release or crisis communication and consider how a company should respond when its reputation is tested. After observing marketing and advertising elements around the UCLA campus, teams refine their work and present a complete product, advertising and PR campaign as one connected system. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Apply the Four Ps of marketing to familiar brands and an original company • Name a product and create its logo, identity and core message • Develop a marketing plan based on audience research and campaign goals • Write slogans and jingles, then select appropriate media channels • Record a 30-second radio ad or storyboard a television commercial • Create PR or crisis materials and present an integrated final campaign

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how audience, positioning, media and the Four Ps shape a campaign • Create connected brand, advertising and public-relations materials for an original company • Present and justify an integrated marketing communications plan Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a brand identity, marketing plan, creative assets and final campaign presentation, plus clearer insight into possible study and careers in strategic communications.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in advertising, branding, marketing, media, design or public relations. It is a strong fit for students who notice why some campaigns stay memorable and want to understand the strategy behind the creative work. Students should be ready to contribute ideas, conduct audience research, create visual and written materials, collaborate on a sustained project and present their decisions. Students should be comfortable using a laptop for campaign development.

title: Artificial Intelligence: Emerging Applications
subject: Computer Science & Technology
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: An AI system can produce an impressive result and still raise difficult questions. Who was represented in the data? What should a person verify? Which decisions require human oversight? Students use these questions to explore how artificial intelligence works and how responsible ideas are designed. Hands-on work covers machine learning, computer vision, gene
description_full: An AI system can produce an impressive result and still raise difficult questions. Who was represented in the data? What should a person verify? Which decisions require human oversight? Students use these questions to explore how artificial intelligence works and how responsible ideas are designed. Hands-on work covers machine learning, computer vision, generative AI, prompt design, and media verification. Students run a human-versus-machine pattern simulation, test a no-code image model with Teachable Machine, compare prompt strategies, and build a checklist for identifying AI-generated media. Case debates and a bias audit introduce fairness, privacy, transparency, accessibility, and possible misuse. Students then develop an original AI for Good concept around a real problem. They define intended users, explain the system at a high level, identify required data, and create a visual prototype or storyboard. An ethics red-team review helps them strengthen safeguards before they pitch the concept and its limitations to a nontechnical audience. They also reflect on what responsible innovation demands from a builder. This two-week full-day academy takes place at UCLA. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Map everyday encounters with AI and identify the system’s role • Run a human-versus-machine pattern-recognition simulation • Test a no-code computer vision model with Teachable Machine • Compare prompts and verify claims in generated output • Audit an AI case for bias, fairness, privacy, and transparency • Prototype and pitch an AI for Good concept with safeguards

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain core ideas behind machine learning, computer vision, and generative AI • Evaluate AI output and system design for evidence, bias, privacy, and human oversight • Design and present an AI concept with clear users, benefits, limits, and safeguards Students will leave with an AI for Good concept and presentation, stronger evaluation and design skills, and greater clarity about continued study or careers involving artificial intelligence.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to understand AI beyond headlines and automated answers. It fits students interested in technology, design, media, ethics, healthcare, education, business, policy, or another area where intelligent systems are changing decisions. Students should be ready to test tools, question results, discuss difficult tradeoffs, collaborate on critiques, and explain an idea to a nontechnical audience. The course will appeal to students who want to explore what AI can do while taking its limits, risks, and human consequences seriously.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain core ideas behind machine learning, computer vision, and generative AI • Evaluate AI output and system design for evidence, bias, privacy, and human oversight • Design and present an AI concept with clear users, benefits, limits, and safeguards Students will leave with an AI for Good concept and presentation, stronger evaluation and design skills, and greater clarity about continued study or careers involving artificial intelligence.

description_full: How would you design a replacement body part that must fit, move and work with a real patient? Students begin by building a life-size anatomy model, then investigate how stem cells, medical devices and engineering can help repair or replace damaged tissues and organs. Design challenges make each body system concrete. Teams develop a prosthetic limb, map how 3D printing supports artificial organs and compare treatment options for kidney failure. They build and test an artificial heart valve, model lungs, investigate liver function and create an ear trumpet while considering hearing technology. Vision simulations and a cochlear-implant discussion add patient experience and ethics to the engineering work. Students document designs and reflections in a science journal while building a capstone proposal for a new application of regenerative medicine. The final project explains the medical need, proposed solution, possible benefits and drawbacks, and connections to areas such as cost, law, education or technology. Students choose a presentation format and share the finished proposal with the class. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Build a life-size body model and connect organs to their functions • Design a prosthetic limb and evaluate its materials and constraints • Research 3D-printed organs and compare kidney-failure treatments • Construct and test an artificial heart valve and lung model • Explore vision, hearing and cochlear-implant questions through simulations and discussion • Propose and present a new regenerative-medicine application

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how selected organs function and how a medical device may support them • Apply an engineering design process to build and evaluate biomedical prototypes • Present a regenerative-medicine proposal that considers benefits, limits and wider effects Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a science journal, several biomedical models and a capstone proposal, plus a clearer sense of what they may want to explore across medicine and engineering.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about the human body, medicine, engineering or how devices can solve health problems. It is a strong fit for students who enjoy building, researching, testing ideas and explaining how a design works. Students should be ready to collaborate on prototypes, record observations, discuss patient and ethical questions respectfully, and develop a project across several checkpoints. The experience can help students identify which medical or engineering questions they want to explore next.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how selected organs function and how a medical device may support them • Apply an engineering design process to build and evaluate biomedical prototypes • Present a regenerative-medicine proposal that considers benefits, limits and wider effects Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a science journal, several biomedical models and a capstone proposal, plus a clearer sense of what they may want to explore across medicine and engineering.

description_full: Passion can start a movement, but lasting change requires a strategy. Students examine how nonprofits, philanthropy, government, businesses, and community organizations approach complex social challenges. Human-centered design, systems thinking, and theory of change provide practical frameworks for moving from a broad concern to an action that can be tested and improved. Case studies and collaborative design challenges ask students to identify stakeholders, examine power dynamics, listen to community perspectives, and define the problem before proposing a solution. They practice creative problem solving, purposeful leadership, impact measurement, and narrative change. Each activity emphasizes evidence and collaboration rather than assuming that one idea or organization can solve a system alone. The work builds toward a student-led community impact day. Teams develop the purpose, audience, partners, activities, responsibilities, and measures that will guide the project. Students also craft a personal leadership narrative that explains the values and experiences they want to bring to future community work. This three-week high school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what they may want to study or pursue next.

description_full: A patient’s symptoms are only the starting point. Students learn how biology, evidence and clinical tools help medical professionals move from an unknown problem toward diagnosis and treatment. The course examines cancer, diabetes, hypertension, kidney disease, meningitis, genetics and causes of death. Simulations and labs make the science concrete: students use a stethoscope and pulse oximeter, take blood pressure, test lung function, explore blood typing and work through disease-detection, diabetes, kidney and concussion scenarios. They also practice suturing and complete Red Cross CPR certification. Visits to a UCLA research lab and undergraduate anatomy lab show additional settings where medical knowledge is developed and applied. Alongside the clinical work, students compare the path to an MD with other careers in healthcare and research. For the capstone, each student investigates a disease’s symptoms, transmission, diagnosis, treatment and prevention, then presents the findings on a research poster. The finished work connects scientific research to clinical communication and career exploration. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Use a stethoscope, pulse oximeter and blood-pressure equipment • Work through simulated diabetes, kidney, meningitis and disease-detection cases • Conduct blood-typing, lung-function and concussion research activities • Practice suturing and complete Red Cross CPR certification • Visit UCLA research and undergraduate anatomy labs • Research a disease and present its diagnosis, treatment and prevention on a poster

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the basic pathology and diagnostic process for several common medical conditions • Use selected clinical tools and apply evidence in simulated patient-care activities • Research and present accurate information about a disease and its management Students will leave with a course completion certificate, Red Cross CPR certification, a disease-research poster and greater clarity about medical study, patient care or health research.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in medicine, biology, patient care or medical research. It is especially relevant for students who want to compare the realities of clinical work with the education and career paths behind it. Students should be ready to learn detailed health-science concepts, participate responsibly in simulations and practical activities, conduct research and present their findings. A prior high school biology course is recommended but not required. Careful, responsible participation matters throughout.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the basic pathology and diagnostic process for several common medical conditions • Use selected clinical tools and apply evidence in simulated patient-care activities • Research and present accurate information about a disease and its management Students will leave with a course completion certificate, Red Cross CPR certification, a disease-research poster and greater clarity about medical study, patient care or health research.

description_full: A small change in measurement, mixing or temperature can completely change a bake. Students learn that lesson through repeated practice, moving from familiar recipes into doughs, meringues, custards and pastry techniques. Each bake connects ingredient choices and technique to structure, flavor and presentation. Students compare results and decide what they would change next. The course begins with no-bake cheesecake, brownies, cookies, muffins and strawberry shortcake. Each recipe introduces a useful skill such as accurate measuring, portioning, whipping cream, decorating or modifying a formula. Students then work with yeast and overnight dough while preparing pita, focaccia and French bread, along with hummus, tomato jam, butter and fruit jams. Later projects add more technical components. Students bake cupcakes with cream-cheese frosting, make pavlovas with crème anglaise and whipped cream, and prepare éclairs and cream puffs with pâte à choux. The sequence gives them experience organizing a recipe, handling ingredients and combining several components into a finished presentation. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Measure, mix and bake brownies, cookies, muffins and shortcakes • Whip cream, prepare frostings and decorate finished desserts • Knead and shape pita, focaccia and French bread dough • Make hummus, tomato jam, fruit jams and fresh butter • Prepare meringue, crème anglaise and composed pavlovas • Bake éclairs and cream puffs using pâte à choux

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply accurate measuring, mixing, kneading and baking techniques across several recipes • Compare how different ingredients and methods affect texture, structure and presentation • Organize multistep bakes that combine dough, filling, sauce or decoration Students will leave with a course completion certificate, practical experience across breads and pastries, and greater clarity about continued study in baking, culinary arts or food entrepreneurship.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and enjoy cooking, baking, working with their hands or understanding why recipes succeed. It is a strong fit for students who want repeated kitchen practice rather than a demonstration-only experience. Students should be ready to follow food-safety and classroom procedures, measure carefully, work through multistep recipes and help keep a shared workspace organized. The course begins with accessible recipes and progresses into breads, custards, meringues and pastry techniques.

Students learn to look behind the headline by reading financial statements, comparing ratios, and asking how a choice affects cash, risk, and long-term value. The course introduces accounting fundamentals, budgeting, forecasting, time value of money, capital budgeting, capital structure, stoc
description_full: A company may be growing and still face a poor financial decision. Students learn to look behind the headline by reading financial statements, comparing ratios, and asking how a choice affects cash, risk, and long-term value. The course introduces accounting fundamentals, budgeting, forecasting, time value of money, capital budgeting, capital structure, stock markets, and risk and return. Applied problem sets and financial cases give students practice using concepts rather than memorizing terms. They analyze company performance, build models in spreadsheets, compare investment opportunities, and participate in stock-market simulations and group decision exercises. The capstone examines artificial intelligence in finance. Students research how AI is used in financial modeling, forecasting, investment analysis, or decision support, then evaluate a real application and present the benefits and limits clearly. The project connects established finance principles to the tools changing how analysts work. Peer questions require them to support claims with finance concepts and distinguish a useful tool from an unsupported promise. This two-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.body: • Read core financial statements and calculate performance ratios • Build budgets, forecasts, and time-value-of-money calculations • Evaluate capital investments and corporate financing choices • Use spreadsheets to create and test financial models • Participate in financial cases and stock-market simulations • Research and present a real application of AI in finance

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze financial statements and ratios to evaluate company performance • Build budgets and models for investment and financing decisions • Explain and assess an AI application in financial analysis Students will leave with applied financial models and an AI-in-finance presentation, stronger quantitative business skills, and greater clarity about continued study or careers in finance, accounting, or analytics.

title: Crack the Code: Mathematics, Ciphers & Encryption
raw_title: Crack the Code: Mathematics, Ciphers & Encryption
subject: Computer Science & Technology
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: A secret message is a mathematical puzzle with a purpose. Students trace cryptography from Caesar shifts and substitution systems to the Enigma machine and the public-key ideas that protect modern communication. Each new cipher reveals both an encoding strategy and a weakness a codebreaker can exploit. Hands-on challenges include building cipher wheels, encr
description_full: A secret message is a mathematical puzzle with a purpose. Students trace cryptography from Caesar shifts and substitution systems to the Enigma machine and the public-key ideas that protect modern communication. Each new cipher reveals both an encoding strategy and a weakness a codebreaker can exploit. Hands-on challenges include building cipher wheels, encrypting and decrypting partner messages, using frequency analysis, and testing Vigenère and Polybius-based systems. Students connect those activities to modular arithmetic, matrices, prime factorization, number theory, and the way computers represent information. Historical cases show how cryptanalysis influenced events and how security standards change when technology advances. For the capstone, students design and analyze an original cryptographic system or complete an in-depth cryptanalysis project. They document the key, method, mathematical reasoning, strengths, limitations, and evidence from testing, then present their findings to the class. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next.

description_full: What makes a short story feel complete even when every word has to earn its place? Students read like writers, examining how character, plot, setting, dialogue, point of view, voice, conflict, and metaphor work together. Short fiction and podcast discussions give the class a practical way to notice techniques that can strengthen their own work. Students develop an original flash-fiction story of about 1,000 words. They practice outlining without becoming trapped by a plan, writing more precise dialogue, using active verbs, and cutting words that slow a scene. A one-minute pitch helps each writer clarify the central idea, while humor, simile, and metaphor exercises expand the choices available during drafting. Revision is treated as part of the creative process. Students submit a first draft, receive individual notes, make focused editing passes, and prepare their story to be read and discussed with the class. They also learn about places writers can submit finished work. This three-week middle school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Identify and apply core fiction techniques in an original story • Revise prose for stronger verbs, clearer dialogue, and more purposeful detail • Discuss how specific writing choices shape a reader’s experience Students will leave with a revised flash-fiction story, a practical editing process, and a clearer sense of which forms of creative writing they may want to explore next.

Students should be ready to read short pieces, write regularly, discuss craft, share work in a supportive setting, and revise a story after receiving feedback. Curiosity and willingness to experiment matter more than having a polished writing style. A completed program application is required.

title: Criminal Psychology: The Roots of Criminal Behavior

description_short: How can criminal psychology help explain criminal behavior and support efforts to prevent it?
