description_full: How can criminal psychology help explain criminal behavior and support efforts to prevent it? Students examine psychodynamic, biological, genetic, social-learning, cognitive, developmental, sociological, and cultural theories. Case studies help them compare these perspectives while exploring violence, aggression, substance-related crime, and the psychological and environmental factors that may shape decision-making. The course places students inside the investigative process through hands-on activities and simulations. They examine fictional crime scenes, interpret witness statements and behavioral evidence, analyze cognitive distortions, map community crime patterns, and compare modus operandi with signature behavior. Profiling challenges and a Behavioral Analysis Unit simulation ask students to connect theory with evidence without treating any one explanation as complete. For the capstone, students serve as criminal psychologists investigating a fictional case. They assemble a Criminal Psychology Case File that includes a case summary, at least three theoretical perspectives, psychological and environmental factors, an offender profile, and prevention or intervention recommendations. Students may develop the work as a report, presentation, or digital portfolio, then present their conclusions in a five-minute evidence-based presentation. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare major psychological, biological, developmental, and social theories of criminal behavior • Investigate a fictional crime scene using witness statements and behavioral evidence • Analyze cognitive distortions, environmental risks, violence, and substance-related crime • Map crime patterns and distinguish modus operandi from signature behavior • Develop an offender profile with prevention or intervention recommendations • Create and present an evidence-based Criminal Psychology Case File

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare psychological, biological, social, and environmental explanations for criminal behavior • Interpret case evidence and behavioral patterns to develop a supported criminal profile • Create and present a case file with evidence-based prevention or intervention recommendations Students leave with a completed Criminal Psychology Case File, stronger investigative and presentation skills, and clearer direction toward further study in psychology, criminal justice, law, or behavioral science.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to examine criminal behavior through psychology, evidence, and hands-on investigation. It fits interests in psychology, criminal justice, law, behavioral science, forensic investigation, or public safety. Participants should be ready to discuss violence, aggression, substance-related crime, and other sensitive subjects in a mature academic setting. They will work with fictional evidence, compare competing theories, participate in simulations, collaborate on case analysis, and present supported conclusions. Students who enjoy solving complex problems and testing ideas against evidence will be especially well matched.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare psychological, biological, social, and environmental explanations for criminal behavior • Interpret case evidence and behavioral patterns to develop a supported criminal profile • Create and present a case file with evidence-based prevention or intervention recommendations Students leave with a completed Criminal Psychology Case File, stronger investigative and presentation skills, and clearer direction toward further study in psychology, criminal justice, law, or behavioral science.

description_full: How can a collection of numbers reveal a pattern, test an idea, or support a prediction? Students begin by asking where data science appears in everyday life, then set up Anaconda and Jupyter notebooks to explore Python syntax, variables, expressions, and data types. Hands-on investigations make statistical thinking concrete. Students review mean, median, mode, and outliers through card-based activities, then use Pandas DataFrames to import, clean, slice, and analyze datasets. They practice removing missing values, isolating columns, creating bar graphs, pie charts, and histograms, and choosing labels and formats that make a visualization clear. As their skills grow, students examine correlation versus causation, consider how interpretation changes a data story, and explore introductory linear regression. Capstone checkpoints guide each student from selecting a dataset and question to building a documented Jupyter notebook with analysis, visualizations, and conclusions. The course concludes with presentations that explain both the findings and the reasoning behind them. This three-week course for middle school students is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus in Los Angeles, California. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Use basic Python syntax and a Jupyter notebook workflow to investigate data • Clean, analyze, and visualize a dataset with Pandas and appropriate graphs • Present a data-supported conclusion while explaining limits in interpretation Students will leave with a capstone Jupyter notebook and a clearer understanding of how programming, statistics, and communication work together in data science.

Students should be ready to practice Python, troubleshoot code, discuss interpretations, and develop a capstone project through several checkpoints. The course begins with foundational Python and Jupyter notebook skills before moving into data analysis. View the eligibility requirements for the Institute for the Gifted on our FAQ page. A completed program application is required.

description_full: How can mathematics help divide something fairly, explain an election result, or find the best route through a network? Students investigate these questions through discrete mathematics, a field built around countable structures, logical relationships, and problems with clear constraints. The course moves through game theory, fair division, election theory, arithmetic and geometric sequences, and several branches of graph theory. Students draw trees, test planar graphs, color maps, trace Euler paths and circuits, and explore matching in bipartite graphs. Later work introduces generating functions and number theory. Exercises, group discussion, and short checks ask students to show how they reached an answer, not simply report one. A capstone gives the sequence a practical purpose. Students select a real-world scenario, model the problem, propose possible solutions, identify factors that could affect the result, and present how discrete mathematics might support future solutions. Three checkpoints support research, application, revision, and reflection. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Test strategies through game-theory problems and examples • Compare methods for fair division and election decisions • Analyze arithmetic and geometric sequences • Draw trees, planar graphs, and bipartite graphs • Solve map-coloring, Euler-path, and matching problems • Model a real-world scenario and present a capstone solution

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply discrete-mathematics methods to constrained problems and real-world scenarios • Analyze graphs, sequences, voting methods, and strategic choices • Model a problem, compare possible solutions, and present a reasoned recommendation Students will leave with a completed capstone analysis, broader exposure to advanced mathematics, and a clearer sense of which mathematical questions they may want to explore next.

Participants should be ready to work through multi-step problems, compare approaches, discuss ideas with classmates, and revise a capstone across several checkpoints. Curiosity and persistence matter because some questions may allow more than one useful method. Gifted course. See Admissions Criteria for eligibility requirements.

description_full: Start with an engineering problem worth investigating, then determine what evidence could move it toward a solution. Students explore the research cycle through questions connected to areas such as biomedical devices, smart cities, sustainable energy, computing, and aerospace. A paper-bridge design challenge makes the process tangible as teams test constraints, compare results, and revise their thinking. Students learn to find and evaluate scholarly sources, choose among experimental, computational, design-based, qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods, and consider ethics in data collection. Workshops in descriptive and inferential statistics, citations, abstracts, data visualization, and peer review help turn an initial idea into a focused research proposal. This hybrid academy combines an on-campus experience with Polygence’s Core Research Program. During the campus program, each student develops an engineering research proposal, abstract, and professional scientific poster, then presents the work in a symposium-style setting. Afterward, students join a virtual cohort and are matched 1:1 with a Polygence research mentor in their field of interest. Across 10 virtual sessions, the mentor helps each student continue the project at an individual pace toward a research paper, symposium presentation, podcast, or another appropriate final format. This 2-week full-day academy takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.body: • Frame an engineering research question around a current technical challenge • Compare experimental, computational, design-based, and mixed research methods • Evaluate scholarly sources and build a focused literature review • Analyze data while considering ethics, limitations, and research integrity • Draft a proposal, abstract, and professional scientific poster • Present an elevator pitch and defend the project at a mock symposium • Continue the project through Polygence’s Core Research Program and 10 one-to-one virtual mentor sessions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Formulate a focused engineering research question and select an appropriate method • Evaluate sources, evidence, ethics, and limitations when developing a proposal • Communicate a research plan through an abstract, scientific poster, and oral presentation Students will leave the campus program with an engineering research proposal and scientific poster, a plan for continuing the project through Polygence mentorship, stronger research and presentation skills, and clearer direction for further study.

curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to investigate how engineers turn questions into evidence-based designs and decisions. It fits students interested in fields such as biomedical, environmental, computer, electrical, mechanical, or aerospace engineering, including those still deciding which direction appeals most. Participants should be ready to read research, work with data, give and receive peer feedback, revise a proposal, and present ideas several times. The experience rewards curiosity, persistence, and thoughtful collaboration. Students should also be ready to continue after the campus program through 10 one-to-one virtual sessions with a Polygence mentor matched to their field of interest.

description_full: What turns a fashion idea into a product people recognize, want, and buy? Students examine the business behind design, tracing how trends, materials, pricing, sourcing, consumer behavior, branding, and merchandising shape what reaches the market. Current industry examples and brand analysis make each decision more concrete. Students build a trend board, compare the life cycle of fashion movements, identify fabrics, and map a product’s path through a global supply chain. Costing exercises show how materials, labor, transportation, and retail markup affect pricing. A mock buying challenge asks teams to balance a target customer, trend forecast, budget, and product assortment, while a social media challenge explores how brands position and promote a collection. The capstone brings these pieces together in a fashion brand launch. Students define a concept or mini collection, identify a target market, create a brand identity, plan products and pricing, and develop a merchandising and marketing strategy before pitching the idea to the class. This three-week high school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what they may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Analyze fashion trends, brands, target customers, and global fashion capitals • Build a trend board using color, fabric, silhouette, and consumer research • Compare materials and consider performance and sustainability • Calculate product costs, retail markups, and pricing decisions • Map a fashion supply chain and make mock retail buying choices • Develop and pitch a fashion brand launch with merchandising and marketing plans

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze how trends, consumers, costs, and supply chains shape fashion products • Apply branding and merchandising principles to a defined target market • Present a fashion brand launch that connects product, pricing, and promotion decisions Students will leave with a trend board and fashion brand launch proposal, stronger commercial judgment, and greater clarity about further study or careers in fashion business.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are curious about fashion, branding, retail, entrepreneurship, or how creative ideas become marketable products. It is a strong fit for students who enjoy tracking trends, analyzing brands, building visual concepts, or making strategic decisions. Students should be ready to research, work with numbers, collaborate on business challenges, and present a developed brand concept. Artistic drawing or sewing experience is not required because the course focuses on the commercial side of fashion. A completed program application is required.

Studio challenges introduce fashion sketching, croquis, color theory, textile properties, fabric identification, hand sewing, and sewing-machine terminology and techniques. Critiques ask them to explain why a material, shape, or detail belongs in the concept and how feedback could strengthen the work. The capstone is an original collection concept. Students bring together a mood board, color story, sketches, brand identity, fabric choices, and construction knowledge, then present and defend their design decisions. The result captures both the creative direction and practical thinking behind the collection. Students also reflect on which studio methods felt most natural and which skills they would need to practice next with greater intention. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. description_full: How does a designer move from inspiration to something another person can wear? Students begin by creating a mood board, learning the elements of design, and sketching outfits on croquis. The process helps them connect line, shape, color, texture, and space to a clear visual idea. The course then moves into construction. Students identify sewing-machine parts, practice straight stitches, backstitches, curves, and pivots, and learn safety procedures. Fabric investigations introduce natural and synthetic materials, grain, drape, texture, pinning, and cutting. Each technique is put to work in a finished project rather than practiced in isolation. Students first sew and decorate a custom bowtie. They then learn zipper types and use a zipper foot to build a personalized pouch. The final vest project introduces reading a pattern, cutting panels, assembling seams, fitting, hemming, and edge finishing. This three-week middle school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Create a mood board and sketch outfit ideas on croquis • Identify design elements and compare fabric properties • Operate a sewing machine safely using foundational stitches • Measure, cut, sew, and decorate a custom bowtie • Install a zipper and construct a personalized fabric pouch • Read a pattern and assemble, fit, hem, and finish a vest

curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Translate a visual concept into fashion sketches and material choices • Use sewing tools and a machine safely to complete basic construction tasks • Follow patterns and construction steps to create finished fabric pieces Students will leave with a mood board, sketches, a bowtie, a zipper pouch, and a vest, plus useful exposure to both fashion design and garment construction.

Students should be ready to follow safety directions, practice techniques before using them in projects, work carefully with tools and fabric, and revise a piece when construction does not go as planned. A completed program application is required.

description_full: A collection begins with a point of view. Students learn how designers turn inspiration into a visual system through mood, color, silhouette, fabric, construction, and the choices that make separate pieces feel connected. Studio challenges introduce fashion sketching, croquis, color theory, textile properties, fabric identification, hand sewing, and sewing-machine terminology and techniques. Critiques ask them to explain why a material, shape, or detail belongs in the concept and how feedback could strengthen the work. The capstone is an original collection concept. Students bring together a mood board, color story, sketches, brand identity, fabric choices, and construction knowledge, then present and defend their design decisions. The result captures both the creative direction and practical thinking behind the collection. Students also reflect on which studio methods felt most natural and which skills they would need to practice next with greater intention. This two-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. description_full: A short film starts long before the camera rolls. Students begin with story, character, and a clear logline, then translate the idea into screenplay pages, storyboards, crew roles, and a filming plan that a team can actually follow. Workshops introduce scene study, audition self-tapes, visual storytelling, producing, directing, camera operation, lighting, sound, and production equipment. Students analyze short films and scripts, revise a screenplay, build a schedule, and rotate through responsibilities in front of and behind the camera. Reviewing dailies helps the group decide what is working and what needs another take. Production continues into editing. Students shape an assembly cut, identify reshoots or voice-over needs, and refine the work through rough-cut and fine-cut stages. Music, sound effects, graphics, and pacing become storytelling choices rather than decoration. The course culminates in an original short film written, performed, directed, produced, and edited by the student team. A final review lets students discuss how their choices changed the story. This three-week full-day academy takes place at UCLA. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Analyze short films and write a logline and screenplay draft • Turn scenes into storyboards, crew roles, and a filming schedule • Practice scene study and record an audition self-tape • Operate camera, lighting, and sound equipment during production • Review dailies and plan reshoots or voice-over recording • Edit assembly, rough, and fine cuts into an original short film

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Develop a short-film concept through screenplay, storyboard, and production planning • Perform and collaborate in defined cast and crew roles during filming • Edit picture, sound, and graphics into a coherent final cut Students will leave with a completed short film, experience across performance and production, and greater clarity about further study or careers in film and entertainment.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to see how stories move from an idea to the screen. It fits aspiring actors, writers, directors, producers, cinematographers, editors, and students who are still deciding which part of filmmaking interests them most. Participants should be ready to give and receive creative feedback, share responsibility for equipment and deadlines, perform or support performers, and keep revising when a scene does not work yet. Students who enjoy storytelling and want substantial experience on both sides of the camera can use the short-film process to test several possible directions.

description_full: How does an idea become a finished film that an audience can watch? Students follow the creative process through film history, screenwriting, storyboarding, acting, production, and editing. Along the way, they learn how directors, writers, performers, camera operators, and editors contribute to the same story. The class develops three short films based on student ideas. Students pitch scripts, shape scenes, plan shots, and rehearse performances before moving into production. Because filmmaking depends on a full crew, students rotate through different responsibilities and learn how preparation, communication, and respect affect what happens on set. Editing lessons then show how pacing and sequence can change the meaning of recorded material. By the end, students have contributed to films from initial concept through post-production and can better identify which parts of the process hold their attention. The experience balances individual creativity with the practical work of making decisions as a team. This three-week middle school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Explore film history and the roles that bring a production together • Pitch story ideas and develop scripts for collaborative short films • Build storyboards that translate written scenes into planned shots • Rehearse and perform scenes while learning on-camera acting basics • Rotate through production responsibilities during classroom film shoots • Edit recorded material into finished short films

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how pre-production, production, and post-production connect • Apply screenwriting, storyboarding, acting, and editing techniques to a film project • Collaborate across creative and production roles to complete a short film Students will leave with experience contributing to three class short films, practical exposure to several filmmaking roles, and a clearer sense of which parts of cinema they want to explore next.

Students should be ready to pitch ideas, take on different production roles, respond respectfully to feedback, and help classmates complete shared projects. A completed program application is required.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how pre-production, production, and post-production connect • Apply screenwriting, storyboarding, acting, and editing techniques to a film project • Collaborate across creative and production roles to complete a short film Students will leave with experience contributing to three class short films, practical exposure to several filmmaking roles, and a clearer sense of which parts of cinema they want to explore next.

description_short: Evidence has value only when investigators can show where it came from, how it was handled and what a scientifically accepted test can support. Students begin with that connection between science and law, then examine how a crime lab identifies physical evidence and works to determine its origin. Case analysis introduces homicide investigation, criminal and
description_full: Evidence has value only when investigators can show where it came from, how it was handled and what a scientifically accepted test can support. Students begin with that connection between science and law, then examine how a crime lab identifies physical evidence and works to determine its origin. Case analysis introduces homicide investigation, criminal and civil law, search and seizure, interviews and the role of the penal code. Students study DNA analysis and the Innocence Project to see both the power of forensic evidence and the consequences of poor laboratory practice. Repeated work with chain of custody emphasizes documentation, contamination prevention and accountability. The course also examines the Seven S’s of crime-scene investigation: secure, separate, scan, see, sketch, search and secure evidence. Students consider tools ranging from evidence markers and forceps to alternate light sources, sifting screens and digital-forensics software. Research, laboratory-style exercises and class presentations connect evidence recovery to reporting and courtroom use. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Analyze homicide and criminal-investigation case studies • Examine how DNA testing can identify or exclude possible sources • Document evidence movement through a defensible chain of custody • Compare presumptive tests, confirmatory tests and laboratory reporting • Apply the Seven S’s of crime-scene investigation to evidence recovery • Evaluate how forensic evidence interacts with law, courts and wrongful convictions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how investigators locate, preserve, test and report physical evidence • Analyze the importance of DNA, scientific standards and chain of custody • Apply a structured crime-scene process to a case or evidence-recovery scenario Students will leave with a course completion certificate, case-analysis and documentation experience, and greater clarity about further study in forensic science, criminal justice or law.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in forensic science, criminal investigation, law or the way physical evidence shapes a case. It is a strong fit for students who enjoy close observation, case analysis and questions with no immediate answer. Students should be ready to discuss serious crimes in an academic setting, keep careful records, compare legal and scientific standards and explain their conclusions. Students should be comfortable engaging with mature case material.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how investigators locate, preserve, test and report physical evidence • Analyze the importance of DNA, scientific standards and chain of custody • Apply a structured crime-scene process to a case or evidence-recovery scenario Students will leave with a course completion certificate, case-analysis and documentation experience, and greater clarity about further study in forensic science, criminal justice or law.

description_short: A crime scene contains more than clues. It contains evidence that must be noticed, collected, preserved, tested, and explained. description_full: A crime scene contains more than clues. It contains evidence that must be noticed, collected, preserved, tested, and explained. Students learn how chemistry, physics, biology, and the scientific method contribute to forensic investigation, then apply those ideas through experiments, role-play, and case analysis. The class studies fingerprints, DNA, blood types and spatter patterns, injury evidence, ballistics, drug residues, fibers, and trace evidence. Students practice bite-mark comparison, test fingerprint methods, analyze simulated blood patterns, and use a pickle-stabbing lab to examine how injury patterns can support an interpretation. Small crime scenes challenge teams to collect evidence carefully and critique one another’s process. A group project develops throughout the course. Teams research a case, form a hypothesis, consider due process, and create a crime scenario for classmates to solve. Legal role-play introduces the perspectives of the defense, plaintiff, detective, and forensic scientist before final case presentations and peer review. This three-week middle school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Observe surroundings and classify different types of forensic evidence • Apply the scientific method to bite-mark and fingerprint investigations • Analyze simulated blood types, spatter patterns, and injury evidence • Examine ballistics, trajectory, drug residues, fibers, and trace evidence • Collect evidence from staged crime scenes and evaluate another team’s process • Build and present a case project for classmates to investigate

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Collect and document simulated evidence using an organized process • Apply scientific observations to compare competing case explanations • Present a case hypothesis that connects evidence, reasoning, and legal context Students will leave with a completed group case project, practical exposure to several forensic methods, and a clearer sense of which parts of science or criminal investigation they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about forensic science, crime-scene investigation, laboratory evidence, or how scientific findings are used in legal cases. It is a strong fit for students who enjoy experiments, puzzles, observation, and debating what evidence supports. Students should be ready to work carefully with simulated evidence, collaborate on a continuing case project, discuss fictional crime scenarios respectfully, and revise an interpretation when new information appears. No prior forensic or legal experience is required. A completed program application is required.

description_full: Why do people form habits, react differently to stress, or remember the same event in different ways? Students explore psychology through the brain, major theories, human development, behavior, emotion, and age-appropriate mental health topics. Activities turn abstract ideas into questions they can observe and discuss. Students build a brain model, separate popular psychology myths from facts, and try a simplified conditioning game inspired by Pavlov. A lifespan timeline introduces development, while emotion charades and nature-versus-nurture discussions show how biology, experience, and social context can interact. Stress-ball construction and calm-down tools connect psychological ideas to everyday choices without treating the class as therapy. Later work introduces common psychological disorders at an age-appropriate level and examines how psychology is used in schools, sports, counseling, and other settings. Mini case-study skits ask teams to apply concepts to realistic situations. For the final project, students choose a real-life question and explain it through art, a skit, video, or short presentation. This three-week middle school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next.

description_full: A startup idea becomes more useful when someone tests the problem behind it. Student teams begin by identifying a real need, writing a focused problem statement, and conducting customer discovery through interviews or surveys. The venture takes shape through market research, customer personas, competitor mapping, and a Lean Canvas. Teams choose acquisition channels, develop a simple marketing plan, and build a minimum viable product as a paper prototype, digital mock-up, or other workable concept. Unit economics, pricing, cost structure, break-even analysis, and a basic financial model force each group to connect ambition with practical choices. The final stage is communication. Students craft a value proposition, build an investor pitch deck, rehearse a concise story, and respond to feedback. A Shark Tank-style showcase gives each team a chance to present its prototype, business model, financial thinking, and customer evidence in a live question-and-answer format. A written reflection helps students identify what they learned while working together as founders. This two-week full-day academy takes place at UCLA. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Identify a real problem and write a focused startup problem statement • Interview or survey potential customers and build target personas • Map competitors and complete a Lean Canvas business model • Create a prototype or minimum viable product mock-up • Calculate pricing, costs, margins, and a basic break-even model • Build and deliver a Shark Tank-style investor pitch

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Validate a startup problem through customer and competitor research • Build a Lean Canvas, prototype, and basic financial model • Present and defend a concise investor pitch with evidence Students will leave with a venture portfolio containing customer findings, a prototype, business and financial models, and a pitch deck, plus greater clarity about entrepreneurial study or careers.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and notice problems, imagine products or services, or want to understand what founders actually do after an idea appears. It fits interests in business, technology, design, marketing, finance, social impact, and innovation. Students should be ready to interview people, share unfinished ideas, work through numbers, divide responsibilities, and revise a concept after direct feedback. The course is especially useful for students who want to test several entrepreneurial roles and learn whether they prefer customer research, product development, strategy, finance, branding, or pitching.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Validate a startup problem through customer and competitor research • Build a Lean Canvas, prototype, and basic financial model • Present and defend a concise investor pitch with evidence Students will leave with a venture portfolio containing customer findings, a prototype, business and financial models, and a pitch deck, plus greater clarity about entrepreneurial study or careers.

subject: Humanities

description_short: A courtroom argument depends on more than confidence. In Hit the Gavel, students explore how attorneys, witnesses, defendants, judges, and jurors contribute to the legal process. Students examine ethical
description_full: A courtroom argument depends on more than confidence. Students need evidence, a clear theory of the case, carefully planned questions, and the ability to respond when testimony changes the direction of a trial. In Hit the Gavel, students explore how attorneys, witnesses, defendants, judges, and jurors contribute to the legal process. Students examine ethical questions in historical case studies, practice legal research, and build skills in opening statements, direct examination, cross-examination, objections, and closing arguments. They take on roles for both the prosecution and defense, learning how the same evidence can lead to competing interpretations. The course culminates in a mock trial based on the fictional events in Holes. Teams investigate whether Camp Green Lake violated child labor protections, prepare witnesses and arguments, and present both sides of the case. A judge and jury then weigh the evidence and reach a decision. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: - Examine how attorneys, witnesses, judges, and jurors contribute to a trial - Analyze evidence and ethical questions in fictional and historical cases - Develop opening statements and closing arguments - Practice direct examination, cross-examination, and objections - Take on roles for both the prosecution and defense - Prepare and present a complete mock trial

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: - Build a legal argument using facts, research, and clear reasoning - Question a witness and respond to competing interpretations of evidence - Speak persuasively while listening and adapting during a live trial - Collaborate in courtroom roles and evaluate a case from more than one perspective Students leave with experience preparing and presenting a full mock trial.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and enjoy debate, public speaking, research, courtroom stories, or questions about fairness and justice. It is a strong fit for students who want to practice thinking on their feet while contributing to a team. Students should be ready to read case materials, take on courtroom roles, question witnesses, listen respectfully, and revise an argument as new evidence appears. Students must bring a laptop or compatible tablet, a charger, and compatible headphones. Institute for the Gifted eligibility requirements apply, and families must submit a completed program application.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: - Build a legal argument using facts, research, and clear reasoning - Question a witness and respond to competing interpretations of evidence - Speak persuasively while listening and adapting during a live trial - Collaborate in courtroom roles and evaluate a case from more than one perspective Students leave with experience preparing and presenting a full mock trial.

description_full: What does it take to welcome a VIP, coordinate hundreds of moving parts, and keep a major event on schedule when something goes wrong? Students examine hospitality and large-scale event production through simulations, case studies, and a live project. The course connects guest experience with the operational decisions that make it possible. Students practice hotel and front-of-house operations, food and beverage coordination, venue selection, accessibility, risk assessment, crowd flow, volunteer management, and service recovery. They design a reception for 500 guests, map logistics for a 10,000-person event, respond to a simulated catering crisis, and draft a run of show that coordinates talent, technology, and operations. Case studies include major sporting and entertainment events in Los Angeles. The capstone is direct work on the Beyond Now Summit, a live speaker conference for high school students. Teams take responsibility for logistics, guest and speaker services, volunteer coordination, media and communications, or event execution. Students complete a rehearsal, contribute during the live event, and present a post-event analysis with a portfolio-ready record of their planning, results, and lessons learned. This two-week high school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what they may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Practice VIP check-in, guest service, and service-recovery decisions • Design food and beverage plans for a large reception • Map venue logistics, accessibility, crowd flow, and risk controls • Draft a run of show with operational cues and contingency time • Recruit and lead volunteers through simulated event challenges • Rehearse, execute, and evaluate a live student speaker summit

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Design hospitality and event plans around guest needs, scale, and operational constraints • Build logistics, risk, volunteer, and run-of-show documents for a live event • Evaluate event execution and present evidence-based improvements Students will leave with a portfolio-ready summit capstone, experience contributing to a live event, and greater clarity about further study or careers in hospitality, events, communications, or operations.

curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are curious about hospitality, event production, guest experience, sports or entertainment operations, communications, or leadership. It is a strong fit for students who enjoy organizing complex projects and seeing a plan become a live experience. Students should be ready to take responsibility within a production team, use shared planning documents, rehearse carefully, respond to real-time challenges, and reflect honestly on results. The live summit requires dependable participation and collaboration across roles. A completed program application is required.

description_full: What does it take to sell a home or manage a residential property? Students build a foundation in real estate while comparing the roles, responsibilities, and daily resources used across the profession. Career exploration introduces the skills behind sales, leasing, property management, contracts, and client communication. Workshops make the process practical. Students practice completing real-estate contracts, distinguish features from benefits, develop a sales pitch, and role-play parts of selling a house. A career exploration fair and possible visit connected to university real-estate resources broaden their view of the industry and the pathways within it. For the capstone, students choose between acting as a real-estate agent selling a home or as a leasing manager running an apartment complex. Teams organize the steps, documents, decisions, and presentation required for their chosen scenario. The project connects professional responsibilities with communication, financial awareness, and the role real estate can play in building wealth. This two-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. description_full: This foundational course introduces students to core principles of leadership through the lens of sports and team dynamics. Discover how legendary teams work together and why some of your favorite athletes are considered such great leaders. Through real-world case studies of notable athletes and teams, students explore essential qualities of successful athletes and leaders, including integrity, communication, resilience, and emotional intelligence, and learn how positive leadership influences team culture and success. The course emphasizes practical skills like supporting teammates, handling challenging situations, and making ethical decisions both on and off the field. Students will develop their own leadership style while learning how great teams function and what makes sports organizations successful. Whether you're team captain, hoping to become one, or just want to be the best teammate possible, this course will help you develop the skills that make a real difference. Learning Outcomes By the end of the course, students will be able to: Demonstrate understanding of core leadership values including integrity, responsibility, and sportsmanship in athletic settings Apply effective communication techniques to improve team dynamics and support fellow athletes Identify and develop personal leadership strengths while recognizing areas for growth as an athlete and teammate Practice decision-making skills that positively impact team culture and performance Analyze how successful teams function and the role each member plays in team success Develop strategies for handling challenges, setbacks, and conflicts in athletic environments Final Project Students will create a "Champion's Playbook" – a personal guide that captures your vision of sports leadership and teamwork, reflecting your personal style and demonstrating what you've learned about being a great teammate and leader. Students should be ready to discuss real-world examples, collaborate with classmates, and reflect on their own approach to leadership and teamwork.

description_full: Why do some brands stay recognizable even when the product, ad, or platform changes? Students investigate how marketing, advertising, and public relations work together to shape what a company offers, how it communicates, and how people respond. Familiar brands and commercials give the class a practical way to examine strategy instead of memorizing definitions. Students apply the four Ps of marketing to a product, analyze logos and brand identity, and invent a product with its own name and visual direction. Advertising exercises explore attention, persuasion, slogans, and story-based messaging. Teams critique existing ads before creating a poster, video script, or jingle for their own campaign. Public relations introduces a different challenge: protecting trust when something goes wrong. Students respond to a fictional company mistake, write a press release or social media post, and decide how the brand should address its audience. The final project combines the product, logo, ad, and PR plan in a full campaign presentation. This three-week middle school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next.

description_short: Begin with a question about medicine or public health, then work backward to determine what evidence could answer it. description_full: Begin with a question about medicine or public health, then work backward to determine what evidence could answer it. Students examine how medical research has developed and learn to search academic databases such as PubMed and the Cochrane Library. Literature-review activities help them compare source quality, identify gaps, and refine broad interests into focused questions and hypotheses. The course introduces PICO, quantitative and qualitative approaches, mixed methods, data collection, and basic analysis. Students consider research integrity, ethics, clinical-trial budgets, and community-engaged participatory research while testing how study design affects the strength and usefulness of a conclusion. Case studies and current health questions provide context for evaluating methods rather than treating research as a fixed recipe. This hybrid academy combines an on-campus experience with Polygence’s Core Research Program. During the campus program, each student develops a medical research proposal, abstract, and professional scientific poster, then presents the work in a symposium-style setting. Afterward, students join a virtual cohort and are matched 1:1 with a Polygence research mentor in their field of interest. Across 10 virtual sessions, the mentor helps each student continue the project at an individual pace toward a research paper, symposium presentation, podcast, or another appropriate final format. This 2-week all-day program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. It is available to residential and commuter students. description_full: Why do some microbes cause disease while others support human health? Students begin by building a microbiology timeline and testing how easily simulated germs move between surfaces. They examine bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, immune responses, and the microbiome through research, games, cases, and presentations. Activities make the science active. Students design a handwashing protocol, map immune cells involved in different disorders, adopt and profile a microbe, practice patient-history questions, investigate antibiotic resistance, and diagnose zoonotic or parasitic infections from case evidence. Disease-transmission and herd-immunity simulations connect individual choices with patterns across a population. A four-part capstone asks each student to identify a challenge involving infectious disease, microbiome research, or biotechnology. Students research the opportunity, propose and compare three solutions, consider pathophysiology and public-health implications, and create a final presentation with visual aids. Peer response and self-reflection help them evaluate both the scientific content and the clarity of their communication. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Build a timeline of discoveries that shaped modern microbiology • Test handwashing methods and model how germs spread through a population • Compare bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, immune responses, and the microbiome • Diagnose infectious-disease cases using patient histories and scientific evidence • Investigate antibiotic resistance, vaccines, zoonoses, and beneficial bacteria • Propose and present a microbial solution with public-health implications

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare major pathogen groups, transmission routes, treatments, and immune responses • Analyze case and simulation evidence to explain infection and disease spread • Propose and present a researched solution to a microbiology or public-health challenge Students will leave with research checkpoints and a visual capstone presentation, useful exposure to medical microbiology, and a clearer sense of which health-science questions they want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about germs, immunity, disease outbreaks, medicine, biotechnology, or public health. It fits students who enjoy asking why an illness spreads, how a treatment works, or when a microbe can be helpful. Participants should be ready to research unfamiliar organisms, discuss health scenarios respectfully, collaborate on simulations and debates, create visual explanations, and revise a capstone after feedback. Curiosity, careful source use, and active participation are the most important preparation.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare major pathogen groups, transmission routes, treatments, and immune responses • Analyze case and simulation evidence to explain infection and disease spread • Propose and present a researched solution to a microbiology or public-health challenge Students will leave with research checkpoints and a visual capstone presentation, useful exposure to medical microbiology, and a clearer sense of which health-science questions they want to explore next.

description_full: What makes a courtroom argument persuasive, and what happens when the other side challenges it? Students examine the roles of attorneys, defendants, witnesses, judges, and jurors before learning the structure and rules that shape a trial. Each topic is connected to a practical question about how a case is prepared and presented. Students work with objections, motions, jury selection, witness testimony, direct and cross-examination, evidence quality, rulings, appeals, jurisdictions, and court levels. Short lessons establish shared legal vocabulary, then application activities and case-study debates ask students to use those concepts in realistic hypothetical situations. Daily notes and discussion encourage them to support claims with clear reasoning. As the course progresses, students practice opening and closing arguments, questioning strategies, and responses to opposing positions. They take on different courtroom perspectives, receive feedback on their reasoning and presentation, and refine how they speak under pressure. The focus is not only on winning an argument, but on understanding procedure and using evidence responsibly. This three-week middle school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare the responsibilities of attorneys, witnesses, judges, jurors, and defendants • Practice objections, motions, and courtroom procedure • Evaluate evidence quality and competing interpretations of a case • Develop questions for direct and cross-examination • Apply jury-selection, jurisdiction, ruling, and appeal concepts • Present and defend arguments in hypothetical case-study debates

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how courtroom roles and trial procedures shape a case • Evaluate evidence and develop questions for witnesses • Present a persuasive legal argument and respond to an opposing position Students will leave with written case notes and experience arguing hypothetical cases, plus a clearer sense of whether law, debate, or public speaking is an interest they want to explore further.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about law, courtroom strategy, debate, evidence, or persuasive speaking. It is a good fit for students who enjoy discussing difficult questions, analyzing different sides of a case, or taking on roles in a structured simulation. Students do not need to be naturally outspoken or have previous debate experience. They should be ready to prepare notes, collaborate with classmates, speak in front of the group, listen to opposing arguments, and revise a position when the evidence changes. A completed program application is required.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how courtroom roles and trial procedures shape a case • Evaluate evidence and develop questions for witnesses • Present a persuasive legal argument and respond to an opposing position Students will leave with written case notes and experience arguing hypothetical cases, plus a clearer sense of whether law, debate, or public speaking is an interest they want to explore further.

description_full: Choosing a stock is only the beginning. Students ask what makes a company worth investigating, how an investor’s goals shape strategy, and why return cannot be considered without risk, fees, and time. The course makes financial ideas visible through articles, videos, group analysis, and portfolio work. Students compare stock-picking criteria, use free screeners, examine company profiles and financial ratios, and build a hypothetical portfolio. As prices change, they calculate return on investment, review allocation choices, and consider how taxes, commissions, interest rates, and different risk profiles affect an outcome. The capstone brings those decisions into one investment presentation. Students document the companies and industries selected, explain their allocation, create a portfolio graphic, track performance, and defend the reasoning behind changes. Students compare results with classmates and revise their reasoning. The goal is not to predict the market. It is to practice making informed choices and explaining the evidence behind them. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Compare stock-picking criteria and connect them to investment goals • Use free stock screeners to research companies and industries • Analyze company profiles, financial ratios, and potential risks • Build a hypothetical portfolio and choose allocations • Track prices and calculate portfolio return on investment • Create and present a capstone investment strategy

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare investments using goals, company information, risk, and financial ratios • Calculate portfolio value and return while accounting for common costs • Present and defend a researched portfolio strategy Students will leave with a tracked hypothetical portfolio and presentation, useful exposure to investing and finance, and a clearer sense of which money topics they want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and ask how the stock market works, why some investments rise or fall, or how people make choices about saving and risk. It fits students interested in money, math, business, current events, or the stories behind well-known companies. Participants should be ready to use basic arithmetic and percentages, research companies, compare ideas with classmates, and explain their decisions. Curiosity and a willingness to revise a strategy matter more than arriving with a favorite stock already chosen.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare investments using goals, company information, risk, and financial ratios • Calculate portfolio value and return while accounting for common costs • Present and defend a researched portfolio strategy Students will leave with a tracked hypothetical portfolio and presentation, useful exposure to investing and finance, and a clearer sense of which money topics they want to explore next.

raw_title: Music Production: Recording, Mixing & Sound Design
subject: Creative Arts
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How does a musical idea become a track that sounds intentional from the first note to the final mix? Students learn the language and workflow of music production while developing original material with digital audio tools. They examine how recording choices, arrangement, editing, effects, and levels influence the sound and emotional impact of a piece. Hands-
description_full: How does a musical idea become a track that sounds intentional from the first note to the final mix? Students learn the language and workflow of music production while developing original material with digital audio tools. They examine how recording choices, arrangement, editing, effects, and levels influence the sound and emotional impact of a piece. Hands-on work introduces digital audio workstations and production software, including Ableton Live, Pro Tools, and Adobe Creative Cloud tools. Students record musical material, organize sessions, edit performances, experiment with sound design, and shape a mix through balance, processing, and revision. The emphasis is on making purposeful choices rather than applying effects without a clear reason. Each student develops original music and moves it through recording, editing, mixing, and mastering. Listening sessions and feedback help students compare approaches, identify technical problems, and refine their own production style. By the end, they can better explain both how a track was built and which parts of the production process they want to study more deeply. This three-week high school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what they may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Learn music production terminology and a digital audio workstation workflow • Record musical material using available microphones, instruments, and digital tools • Arrange and edit audio into a structured production session • Experiment with sound design, effects, and processing choices • Balance levels and refine a mix through focused listening and feedback • Master and present an original finished track

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply a digital audio workstation workflow to record and organize a project • Edit, process, and mix audio using purposeful technical choices • Complete and explain an original track from initial idea through mastering Students will leave with an original finished track, stronger production and listening skills, and greater clarity about further study or possible pathways in music, audio technology, or media.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to understand how original music is recorded, edited, mixed, and prepared as a finished track. It is a strong fit for students interested in songwriting, beat making, audio technology, performance, or the production decisions behind the music they hear. Students should be ready to experiment, listen closely, revise technical and creative choices, and develop an original project over time. Familiarity with music can help, but advanced performance or production experience is not required. A completed program application is required.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply a digital audio workstation workflow to record and organize a project • Edit, process, and mix audio using purposeful technical choices • Complete and explain an original track from initial idea through mastering Students will leave with an original finished track, stronger production and listening skills, and greater clarity about further study or possible pathways in music, audio technology, or media.

title: Psychology Academy
subject: Psychology & Social Science
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: Psychology asks students to examine familiar behavior with unfamiliar precision. Why do people remember, conform, judge, cope, or make decisions as they do? Students compare explanations from social, cognitive, forensic, health, and abnormal psychology while learning how researchers test those ideas. Lectures, research articles, and classroom activities intr
description_full: Psychology asks students to examine familiar behavior with unfamiliar precision. Why do people remember, conform, judge, cope, or make decisions as they do? Students compare explanations from social, cognitive, forensic, health, and abnormal psychology while learning how researchers test those ideas. Lectures, research articles, and classroom activities introduce scientific method, research ethics, methodology, empirical analysis, and academic writing. In groups, students develop a novel research question, review relevant literature, design a method, collect class data, and interpret the results. The project makes it possible to see where a finding is strong, where a design is limited, and how evidence differs from an appealing assumption. Each group communicates its investigation in an APA-style research paper and presentation. Students organize the question, methods, analysis, and conclusions, then explain how the work connects to psychological theory. Career discussions also help them compare research, clinical, and other directions across the field. Individual reflection helps each student identify the questions and roles they want to investigate further. This two-week full-day academy takes place at UCLA. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare theories from social, cognitive, forensic, health, and abnormal psychology • Read empirical research and evaluate questions, methods, and evidence • Develop a novel group research question and literature review • Design a method and collect class data ethically • Analyze results and identify limitations in the research design • Write an APA-style paper and present the group study

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare major psychological perspectives and apply them to behavior • Design and evaluate an ethical psychological research study • Analyze data and communicate findings in an APA-style paper and presentation Students will leave with a completed group research project, stronger scientific and academic-writing skills, and greater clarity about continued study or careers in psychology and social science.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade curious about behavior, thought, emotion, mental health, or the research behind psychological claims. It fits students considering psychology, social science, healthcare, law, education, business, or another field concerned with how people think and act. Students should be ready to read research, participate in discussion, work closely with a group, collect and analyze class data, and write in a structured academic format. The course is especially useful for students who want both a broad introduction to psychological perspectives and firsthand experience conducting a small research study.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare major psychological perspectives and apply them to behavior • Design and evaluate an ethical psychological research study • Analyze data and communicate findings in an APA-style paper and presentation Students will leave with a completed group research project, stronger scientific and academic-writing skills, and greater clarity about continued study or careers in psychology and social science.

The work makes engineering tangible because every design choice has to function as well as look intentional. Studen
description_full: Start with a sketch, a pile of ordinary materials, and a question: how can code make this creation move or respond? Students combine craft supplies or recycled materials with a Hummingbird robotics kit to turn an idea into an interactive robot. The work makes engineering tangible because every design choice has to function as well as look intentional. Students plan, build, program, test, and revise their creations. They use text-based languages such as JavaScript and Python to control behavior, then troubleshoot when the physical build and the code do not work together as expected. Possible projects include an interactive display, a model inspired by a favorite myth, or a responsive creature for a robotic zoo. The project develops through repeated cycles of construction and debugging. Students make creative decisions, solve technical problems, and learn how programmers and engineers improve a prototype. By the end, each student has a personally meaningful robotic creation that combines coding, engineering, and craftsmanship. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next. A supplemental course fee of $295 applies.

curriculum_sections.body: • Sketch a personally meaningful robot and plan how it should move or respond • Build a robot using craft or recycled materials and a Hummingbird kit • Write JavaScript or Python code to control interactive behavior • Test connections between the physical design and the program • Debug technical problems and revise the robot through repeated trials • Create an interactive display, story-based model, or robotic zoo creature

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Design and construct a creative robot that responds through programmed behavior • Apply JavaScript or Python to control and revise an interactive build • Test, troubleshoot, and improve a prototype using engineering problem-solving Students will leave with a personally meaningful robotic creation, practical exposure to coding and engineering, and a clearer sense of which parts of robotics they may want to explore next.

Students should be ready to work with text-based code, test ideas repeatedly, solve problems, and revise a physical creation. description_full: Every speech asks an audience to think, feel, do, or remember something. Students learn how informative, persuasive, entertaining, and ceremonial speeches serve those different purposes. They analyze hooks, evidence, stories, tone, pacing, body language, and visuals to see how a speaker earns attention and credibility. Short, low-stakes speaking activities build toward more sustained work. Students tell an impromptu two-minute story, examine professional speeches and advertisements, organize ideas in an outline, and practice vocal delivery and audience awareness. Workshops, structured discussions, and peer critique help them revise both the message and the way they present it. For the capstone, each student develops and delivers a ten-minute speech about a topic they care about. The format may be a demonstration, dramatic reading, persuasive or special-occasion speech, debate, or congressional-style argument. Students research, submit a written outline, rehearse, revise from feedback, and make purposeful choices about how they want the audience to respond. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Compare informative, persuasive, entertaining, and ceremonial speeches • Analyze hooks, evidence, stories, tone, pacing, body language, and visuals • Practice impromptu speaking and audience-focused delivery • Organize research and ideas in a written speech outline • Give and apply specific peer feedback during workshops • Rehearse and deliver a ten-minute capstone speech
