description_full: Could time travel work without breaking the laws of physics? Students investigate that question by comparing ideas from quantum mechanics, general relativity, and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. Black holes, negative energy, cosmic strings, and spacetime become entry points for asking what current physics allows and where the hardest questions remain. Students examine experiments and scientific arguments that have shaped modern thinking about time. They analyze classic time-travel paradoxes, consider the possibility of mutable timelines, and test competing explanations through thought experiments and debate. The goal is not to treat science fiction as fact, but to use an imaginative problem to practice careful reasoning about evidence, assumptions, and consequences. The course builds toward an original time-travel theory. Students decide which physical ideas support their proposal, identify the paradoxes it must address, and explain where evidence ends and speculation begins. Sharing and defending that theory helps them communicate complex ideas clearly while discovering how physics, philosophy, and science fiction approach the nature of time from different angles. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare quantum mechanics, general relativity, and quantum gravity • Investigate black holes, negative energy, cosmic strings, and spacetime • Analyze time-travel paradoxes and the idea of mutable timelines • Examine experiments and evidence connected to theories of time • Test competing ideas through thought experiments and debate • Develop and explain an original theory of time travel

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare major physics ideas connected to spacetime and time travel • Analyze paradoxes, evidence, and assumptions within a scientific argument • Construct and explain an original theory of time travel Students leave with a personal time-travel theory, a Summer Discovery certificate of completion, and a clearer sense of which questions in physics they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about physics, black holes, spacetime, time-travel stories, or questions that do not have simple answers. It fits students who enjoy testing unusual ideas, looking for logical contradictions, and discussing different explanations with classmates. Students should be ready to engage with challenging concepts, participate in thought experiments and debate, and explain a theory of their own. Institute for the Gifted eligibility requirements apply. Families should review the criteria on the FAQ page and submit a completed program application.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare major physics ideas connected to spacetime and time travel • Analyze paradoxes, evidence, and assumptions within a scientific argument • Construct and explain an original theory of time travel Students leave with a personal time-travel theory, a Summer Discovery certificate of completion, and a clearer sense of which questions in physics they may want to explore next.

description_full: A strong business idea starts with a problem worth solving. Students look for unmet needs, test whether an idea could create real value, and narrow their thinking to one original venture concept. Course content is powered by the Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) and uses NFTE’s nationally recognized curriculum and Entrepreneurial Mindset framework. Students organize their idea with a Lean Business Model Canvas, conduct primary and secondary market research, define a target customer, and estimate demand. Competitive analysis, a SWOT evaluation, and human-centered design help them sharpen their value proposition. Branding and marketing workshops turn that strategy into a message customers can understand. Students then examine fixed and variable costs, pricing, revenue models, unit economics, and break-even points. Using the NFTE Business Workbook and pitch-deck framework, they assemble their research and decisions into a professional presentation. The course culminates in a Fast Pitch Challenge evaluated with NFTE’s official rubric, followed by questions and structured feedback from instructors and experienced entrepreneurs. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes

Students should be ready to collaborate, study potential customers, work with basic calculations, revise their thinking, and present to an audience. The course guides students through the NFTE process from identifying a problem to delivering a final pitch.

description_full: Why do some digital campaigns earn attention while others disappear in the feed? Students begin by defining a target audience and brand objective, then examine how entertainment, sports, media, and consumer brands use positioning and storytelling to build interest. The academy moves from strategy into production. Students develop campaign concepts, plan content for different platforms, write ad copy, create sample visual and video assets, and consider how influencer partnerships can extend a message. They also work with measures such as reach, engagement, and conversion to judge performance and recommend changes. Case discussions, workshops, critique, and revision show how creative choices and business goals shape one another. The work builds toward an individual digital campaign portfolio for a selected brand or entertainment property. Students bring together an audience profile, campaign objective, positioning idea, channel plan, sample content, measurement framework, and data-informed recommendations, then present the strategy and explain their decisions. This three-week full-day high school academy takes place at UCLA Anderson School of Management in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA Anderson and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what they may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Define a target audience, campaign objective, and brand position • Analyze digital campaigns from entertainment, sports, media, and consumer brands • Plan platform-specific content and write persuasive ad copy • Create sample visual and video assets for a campaign • Interpret reach, engagement, and conversion metrics • Build and present an individual digital campaign portfolio

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Develop a digital campaign strategy for a defined audience and objective • Create platform-appropriate content that supports a clear brand position • Analyze campaign metrics and recommend evidence-based improvements Students will leave with a digital campaign portfolio, stronger strategic and creative skills, and greater clarity about studying or pursuing marketing, advertising, media, or business.

curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in advertising, social media, brand strategy, content creation, entertainment, sports, or consumer behavior. Students must demonstrate academic achievement with mostly A and/or B grades in their high school courses. Students should be ready to discuss campaign examples, create and revise content, interpret basic performance data, collaborate during workshops, and explain the reasoning behind their choices. The experience can help students decide whether they want to explore marketing, advertising, media, analytics, or business more deeply.

description_full: What should a company do when the market changes, the numbers are uncertain, and a team disagrees about the next move? Students step into that tension through business cases and simulations that ask them to weigh evidence, choose a strategy, and explain the tradeoffs. The academy builds a foundation across strategy, finance, and leadership. Students use SWOT and competitive analysis, read basic financial statements, compare business models, and examine how organizations create value. Leadership workshops add communication, ethical decision-making, teamwork, and conflict resolution. Students practice adapting their approach to different situations and use feedback and reflection to identify their own strengths and areas for growth. For the capstone, teams act as management consultants for an entertainment-industry company facing a significant challenge. They define the problem, study the company and market, consider financial and ethical implications, develop a recommendation, and present their reasoning. The project brings together the analytical and interpersonal skills used throughout the academy. This three-week full-day high school academy takes place at UCLA Anderson School of Management in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA Anderson and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what they may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Analyze business cases and identify the decisions leaders must make • Use SWOT and competitive analysis to evaluate a company’s position • Read basic financial statements and connect numbers to strategy • Compare leadership styles through simulations and team challenges • Practice ethical decision-making, communication, and conflict resolution • Develop and present a team consulting recommendation

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze a business challenge using strategic and financial evidence • Apply leadership, communication, and ethical reasoning to team decisions • Present a clear consulting recommendation and defend its tradeoffs Students will leave with a consulting presentation, stronger business and leadership skills, and greater clarity about studying or pursuing business, management, entrepreneurship, or organizational leadership.

Cases and simulations introduce the economics of sports and the roles of strategy, finance, marketing, media rights, sponsorship, operations, and analytics. Teams then identify a sports-business challenge and develop a practical response. description_short: What could you build with AI if the goal were to improve something you care about? The course focuses on using AI thoughtfully to move from an idea to a working product. Step-by
description_full: What could you build with AI if the goal were to improve something you care about? Students explore current generative AI tools, identify a social problem, and develop an original project from a blank page. No programming or computer science background is required. The course focuses on using AI thoughtfully to move from an idea to a working product. Step-by-step workshops introduce ChatGPT or Claude, Lovable, and Cursor. Students learn how large language models generate responses, how AI agents can carry out connected tasks, and how retrieval-augmented generation and context engineering help a system use the right information. They practice prompting, testing, revising, and using vibe coding to turn plain-language instructions into product features. During the second half, each student builds an individualized project with measurable social impact. Topics may include health and mental health, financial inclusion, engineering, sustainability, or education. Students define the purpose and target users, decide how they will measure impact, test the concept, and refine the product. They finish by assessing market fit and pitching the project in a format that can support competitions, research fairs, or a college portfolio. This two-week course is part of Summer Discovery at the University of Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Explore ChatGPT or Claude, Lovable, and Cursor through guided workshops • Examine how large language models, AI agents, and retrieval tools work • Use prompting, context engineering, and vibe coding to build product features • Define a social problem, target users, and measurable impact • Test an individualized AI product and assess its market fit • Pitch the finished project for feedback and future opportunities

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how generative AI models, agents, retrieval, and context shape product behavior • Apply prompting and vibe-coding methods to build and improve an AI product • Present a social-impact project with defined users, impact measures, and market fit Students will leave with an original AI product and pitch they can continue refining for competitions, research fairs, or college portfolios, plus greater clarity about further study in AI or product development.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are curious about generative AI and want to build something connected to a real issue. subject: Computer Science & Technology
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: What separates an AI user from an AI builder? Students learn Python fundamentals and the structure of modern artificial intelligence, including models, tools, agents, and systems. Interactive talks, whiteboard activities, demonstrations, and coding labs connect concepts with the practical choices involved in building with data. Projects move through classifi
description_full: What separates an AI user from an AI builder? Students learn Python fundamentals and the structure of modern artificial intelligence, including models, tools, agents, and systems. Interactive talks, whiteboard activities, demonstrations, and coding labs connect concepts with the practical choices involved in building with data. Projects move through classification, decision trees, bias audits, neural networks, computer vision, multimodal systems, natural language processing, word embeddings, large language models, and prompt engineering. Students train and evaluate models, interpret outputs with tools such as saliency maps, explore semantic search, and build a tool-calling agent that can take defined actions. In small groups, students select an AI for Social Good problem while each student builds and deploys a custom application. The project cycle includes data exploration, model building, evaluation, iteration, ethics, and presentation. Final work includes a live app and Demo Day presentation, supported by workshops on AI research and responsible project communication. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Use Python to explore and manipulate a real-world dataset • Train a decision tree and conduct a bias audit • Build and stress-test an image classifier • Explore embeddings, semantic search, and prompt-engineering strategies • Create a tool-calling AI agent and application workflow • Build, deploy, and present an AI for Social Good app

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Train and evaluate introductory machine-learning models using Python • Build an AI agent or application with defined tools and responsible constraints • Develop, deploy, and present an evidence-tested AI project Students leave with a live AI application, project presentation, and stronger skills in coding, evaluation, ethics, and deployment.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend

Participants should be ready for hands-on Python work, model testing, teamwork, ethical discussion, and iterative app development. Optional preparation materials support Python and AI basics, and mentors balance challenge with approachability. Persistence and willingness to debug are important.

description_full: How can advertising connect a community issue with an audience that can act? Students examine advertising’s influence on culture, public opinion, and consumer behavior. Case studies of iconic brands and social campaigns reveal how emotion, positioning, segmentation, and market research shape who notices a message and how they respond. Hands-on activities ask students to analyze target markets, compare campaign effectiveness, and work with digital advertising. They investigate the social, cultural, and economic context of Ann Arbor, then choose a local business or nonprofit and define a target demographic, communication challenge, and possible community partners. The capstone is a community-centered campaign. Students set goals, develop messaging and tactics, and create materials across multiple media such as social content, web pages, video, print, or billboards. The final presentation explains the research, strategic choices, creative execution, and way the campaign supports both the organization and a relevant local issue. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Analyze how advertising influences culture and consumer behavior • Research a local organization, community issue, and target audience • Apply segmentation and positioning to a campaign strategy • Evaluate factors behind campaign success or failure • Create advertising assets across multiple media • Present and defend a community-centered campaign

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze how audience insight and positioning shape campaign strategy • Develop coordinated advertising across appropriate channels • Evaluate and present a campaign using strategic and creative evidence Students leave with a multi-channel campaign and experience applying advertising strategy to a real Ann Arbor community context.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in advertising, consumer behavior, brands, social issues, design, or digital media. It fits students who want to combine audience research with creative execution. Participants should be ready to research a local organization, collaborate, create in more than one medium, and explain how their choices support a strategy. Curiosity about culture and community will strengthen the work.

title: Biopsychology, Cognition, and Neuroscience (BCN)
subject: Medicine & Health Sciences
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How do electrical signals, chemical processes, genes, and experience shape the brain and behavior? Students explore the cross-disciplinary field of biopsychology, cognition, and neuroscience. Topics include neuronal communication, brain structure, neuroplasticity, sensory and perceptual processes, learning, memory, language, decision-making, and emerging res
description_full: How do electrical signals, chemical processes, genes, and experience shape the brain and behavior? Students explore the cross-disciplinary field of biopsychology, cognition, and neuroscience. Topics include neuronal communication, brain structure, neuroplasticity, sensory and perceptual processes, learning, memory, language, decision-making, and emerging research. Interactive work makes difficult concepts tangible. Students model neurons, simulate impulse conduction and action potentials, map brain regions, test mirror tracing and reaction time, measure reflexes, and compare memory strategies such as repetition, deep processing, and chunking. Each activity connects biological mechanisms with observable behavior and research questions. For the capstone, students complete a systematic review of an area in biopsychology or neuroscience using primary research. They identify gaps in current knowledge and may propose an experiment, then organize their work into scientific sections including methods, results, discussion, and references. A presentation and research report communicate the question, evidence, and future direction. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Model neuronal structure and simulate action-potential conduction • Map brain regions and investigate effects of lobe damage • Test neuroplasticity through a mirror-tracing activity • Measure reaction time, reflexes, and lateral preferences • Compare memory strategies including repetition and deep processing • Complete and present a systematic review of current neuroscience research

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how neuronal communication and brain systems support behavior • Analyze learning, memory, perception, and cognition through biological evidence • Synthesize primary research and identify a meaningful gap for future study Students leave with completed experimental activities, a scientific review and presentation, and a stronger framework for understanding the brain and behavior.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in neuroscience, psychology, biology, medicine, cognition, or research. It fits students who want both hands-on demonstrations and a rigorous introduction to reading scientific literature. Participants should be ready to work through biological mechanisms, collect and interpret simple data, collaborate on activities, and complete substantial research. The capstone expects sustained engagement with primary sources, making the course a strong fit for academically motivated students. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how neuronal communication and brain systems support behavior • Analyze learning, memory, perception, and cognition through biological evidence • Synthesize primary research and identify a meaningful gap for future study Students leave with completed experimental activities, a scientific review and presentation, and a stronger framework for understanding the brain and behavior.

description_short: How do electrical signals, chemical processes, genes, and experience shape the brain and behavior? Topics include neuronal communication, brain structure, neuroplasticity, sensory and perceptual processes, learning, memory, language, decision-making, and emerging res
description_full: How do electrical signals, chemical processes, genes, and experience shape the brain and behavior? Students explore the cross-disciplinary field of biopsychology, cognition, and neuroscience. Topics include neuronal communication, brain structure, neuroplasticity, sensory and perceptual processes, learning, memory, language, decision-making, and emerging research. Interactive work makes difficult concepts tangible. Students model neurons, simulate impulse conduction and action potentials, map brain regions, test mirror tracing and reaction time, measure reflexes, and compare memory strategies such as repetition, deep processing, and chunking. Each activity connects biological mechanisms with observable behavior and research questions. For the capstone, students complete a systematic review of an area in biopsychology or neuroscience using primary research. They identify gaps in current knowledge and may propose an experiment, then organize their work into scientific sections including methods, results, discussion, and references. A presentation and research report communicate the question, evidence, and future direction. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

description_full: Passion can start a movement, but lasting change requires a strategy. Students examine how nonprofits, philanthropy, government, businesses, and community organizations approach complex social challenges. Human-centered design, systems thinking, and theory of change provide practical frameworks for moving from a broad concern to an action that can be tested and improved. Case studies and collaborative design challenges ask students to identify stakeholders, examine power dynamics, listen to community perspectives, and define the problem before proposing a solution. curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze a social challenge across stakeholders, systems, and power relationships • Apply human-centered design and theory of change to an impact strategy • Plan and evaluate a collaborative community action project Students will leave with a community impact plan and personal leadership narrative, stronger tools for leading change, and greater clarity about further study or pathways in public service, social impact, or community leadership.

description_full: Mechanical engineer, aerospace engineer, robotics designer, civil engineer, biomedical engineer, or systems engineer: which path fits a student’s strengths and interests? Students compare careers across engineering disciplines while examining the coursework, extracurricular preparation, and professional training that different pathways require. The course connects careers with major issues shaping the field. Discussions address sustainable design, space exploration, automation and robotics, infrastructure and public safety, materials innovation, and the ethical responsibilities engineers carry when their work affects people and the environment. Guest speakers add perspectives from industry, research, government, and entrepreneurial roles. For the capstone, teams choose an engineering discipline and design a project that addresses a real-world problem, following it from concept through prototype and presentation. Each project considers technical requirements, constraints and trade-offs, testing and iteration, and career paths connected to the specialty, including research, design, manufacturing, consulting, or startup founding. Students present their projects, explain their interest in the discipline, and use feedback to strengthen their reasoning and technical communication. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare training, responsibilities, and daily work across engineering disciplines • Examine sustainability, safety, ethics, and innovation questions engineers face • Research design, manufacturing, consulting, and entrepreneurial engineering roles • Define requirements, constraints, and trade-offs for a real-world problem • Design, prototype, test, and improve a team engineering solution • Present the project and a researched engineering career pathway

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare engineering disciplines by training, responsibilities, and professional pathways • Apply engineering design principles, including constraints, trade-offs, testing, and iteration • Evaluate ethical, safety, and sustainability considerations and present a project-based career plan Students will leave with a completed design project and clearer next steps for exploring mechanical engineering, aerospace engineering, and the broader field.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in mechanical engineering, aerospace engineering, robotics, civil engineering, biomedical engineering, or the field more broadly. It fits students who want to compare disciplines before choosing a direction. No prior engineering coursework is required. Students should be ready to research career pathways, discuss design trade-offs and engineering ethics respectfully, work through hands-on design challenges, collaborate, and present. Curiosity about how things are designed, built, tested, and improved will be valuable. The experience can help students identify which engineering questions and pathways they may want to explore more deeply.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare engineering disciplines by training, responsibilities, and professional pathways • Apply engineering design principles, including constraints, trade-offs, testing, and iteration • Evaluate ethical, safety, and sustainability considerations and present a project-based career plan Students will leave with a completed design project and clearer next steps for exploring mechanical engineering, aerospace engineering, and the broader field.

title: Careers in Law: Introduction to the US Legal System
raw_title: Careers in Law: Introduction to the US Legal System
subject: Law & Government
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How can one legal decision change behavior far beyond a courtroom? Students examine the American criminal justice system through the perspectives of courts, law-enforcement officials, victims, offenders, and different communities. The course connects English common law and constitutional law with contemporary questions affecting high school and college stude
description_full: How can one legal decision change behavior far beyond a courtroom? Students examine the American criminal justice system through the perspectives of courts, law-enforcement officials, victims, offenders, and different communities. The course connects English common law and constitutional law with contemporary questions affecting high school and college students. Discussions, readings, and problems address academic integrity, substance use, reputation and social media, bullying, and a teenager’s place in the legal system. Students compare objective facts with competing interpretations and examine how race, age, gender, politics, and institutional roles can affect experiences of justice. For the capstone, students select a landmark criminal court decision, with or without a related Supreme Court ruling. They research the background, verdict, reasoning, and social impact, then predict how future decisions using the precedent could affect society. A multimedia presentation communicates the analysis and supports the prediction with legal evidence. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Map perspectives within the American criminal justice system • Examine how common law and constitutional law evolved • Discuss legal dilemmas involving students and social media • Research the background and reasoning of landmark decisions • Evaluate how a verdict changed behavior or institutions • Present a precedent-based prediction through multimedia

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how courts, law enforcement, victims, and offenders interact within criminal justice • Analyze a landmark decision using facts, reasoning, precedent, and social impact • Develop and defend a prediction about how legal precedent may shape future cases Students leave with a completed landmark-case analysis and stronger skills in legal research, precedent, civic reasoning, and multimedia advocacy.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in law, criminal justice, government, history, policy, or civic debate. It fits students who want to understand how court decisions shape society. Participants should be ready to read legal material, discuss contested issues respectfully, compare different perspectives, research a landmark case, and deliver a multimedia presentation. Evidence-based reasoning and intellectual openness will support success. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how courts, law enforcement, victims, and offenders interact within criminal justice • Analyze a landmark decision using facts, reasoning, precedent, and social impact • Develop and defend a prediction about how legal precedent may shape future cases Students leave with a completed landmark-case analysis and stronger skills in legal research, precedent, civic reasoning, and multimedia advocacy.

description_full: What makes a rule fair, and how should courts apply it when rights, safety, and community interests collide? Students enter the American legal system through the rule of law, constitutional principles, the Bill of Rights, and the relationship between common and constitutional law. Landmark decisions become daily case studies for identifying facts, evaluating reasoning, and tracing how precedent shapes public life. The course then turns to contemporary criminal-justice questions that affect young people and communities. Students examine juvenile justice, school discipline, restorative justice, cyberbullying, policing, victimology, reentry, and root causes of crime. Discussion, research, and case presentations build legal vocabulary while helping students separate evidence from assumption and compare competing interpretations. For the capstone, each student selects a landmark criminal decision and investigates its background, verdict, reasoning, and social impact. A multimedia presentation asks students to explain the case clearly and predict how its precedent could influence future disputes. The result is practical experience with research, argument, and public speaking. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Examine the rule of law, constitutional principles, and the Bill of Rights • Brief landmark cases by identifying facts, issues, rulings, and reasoning • Debate contemporary questions involving schools, technology, policing, and juvenile justice • Compare punitive, rehabilitative, and restorative approaches to crime and conflict • Research the history, social impact, and future influence of a legal precedent • Present a multimedia criminal-justice capstone and respond to audience questions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze landmark decisions by separating facts, legal questions, reasoning, and precedent • Evaluate criminal-justice issues using evidence and competing legal or community perspectives • Research and present a reasoned argument about a case’s social and future impact Students will leave with a multimedia case presentation, stronger legal-reasoning and communication skills, and clearer insight into further study or careers connected to law and justice.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in law, criminal justice, government, history, policy, or civic debate. It fits students who want to understand how court decisions shape society. Participants should be ready to read legal material, discuss contested issues respectfully, compare different perspectives, research a landmark case, and deliver a multimedia presentation. Evidence-based reasoning and intellectual openness will support success. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze landmark decisions by separating facts, legal questions, reasoning, and precedent • Evaluate criminal-justice issues using evidence and competing legal or community perspectives • Research and present a reasoned argument about a case’s social and future impact Students will leave with a multimedia case presentation, stronger legal-reasoning and communication skills, and clearer insight into further study or careers connected to law and justice.

description_full: Doctor, nurse, hospital administrator, pharmacist, dentist, or vaccine researcher: which role fits which strengths and goals? Students compare careers across medicine and health science while examining the coursework, extracurricular preparation, and professional training required for different pathways. The course connects careers with major issues shaping healthcare. Discussions address medical ethics, health disparities, biomedical research, healthcare costs and reform, personal wellness, and mental health. Guest speakers and possible visits to University of Michigan medical facilities add perspectives from clinical, research, administrative, and commercial roles. For the capstone, teams choose a profession and create three or four fictional cases following people from different backgrounds through career decisions. Each case addresses academic requirements, extracurricular preparation, branching paths, wellness, and possible roles in research, leadership, consulting, or biotechnology. Students present the cases and explain their own interest in the selected profession. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students test their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare education and responsibilities across healthcare careers • Examine medical ethics, disparities, costs, and healthcare reform • Research clinical, administrative, biotechnology, and research roles • Develop a care plan for a complex patient scenario • Learn from healthcare professionals and medical facilities when available • Create and present a case-based career pathway project

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare healthcare professions by responsibilities, education, and professional pathways • Analyze ethical, equity, wellness, and system considerations in healthcare • Develop and present researched career cases for a selected health profession Students leave with a completed case-based career project and clearer next steps for exploring medicine, health science, research, and healthcare leadership.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in medicine, nursing, research, dentistry, pharmacy, hospital leadership, biotechnology, or public health. It fits students who want to compare options before choosing a direction. Participants should be ready to research professional pathways, discuss complex healthcare issues respectfully, analyze patient cases, collaborate, and present. Curiosity about both patient care and the wider healthcare system will be valuable. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: Why do some people manipulate, deceive, exploit, or kill, and how can those behaviors be studied without glamorizing harm? Students examine criminal psychology through psychodynamic, biological, developmental, cognitive, social-learning, sociological, and cultural theories. Cases and media analysis reinforce the difference between explaining behavior and exc
description_full: Why do some people manipulate, deceive, exploit, or kill, and how can those behaviors be studied without glamorizing harm? Students examine criminal psychology through psychodynamic, biological, developmental, cognitive, social-learning, sociological, and cultural theories. Cases and media analysis reinforce the difference between explaining behavior and excusing it. Activities ask students to sort fictional cases by theory, compare strong and weak explanations, and analyze motive, behavior, evidence, and harm in film, television, and case studies. Discussion of profiling and true-crime media focuses on ethical limits, unsupported assumptions, and the responsibilities involved in telling stories about victims and offenders. For the capstone, students investigate a real or fictional criminal subject and create a short podcast. They use multiple psychological theories, distinguish evidence from speculation, and consider how different explanations address development, identity, or motivation. The final product combines compelling storytelling with responsible analysis grounded in criminal psychology. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Sort fictional cases across major theories of criminal behavior • Compare biological, developmental, cognitive, and social explanations • Analyze criminal subjects in film, television, and case studies • Evaluate ethical limits in profiling and true-crime storytelling • Research a real or fictional criminal subject • Produce a podcast grounded in theory, evidence, and ethical analysis

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare major psychological and social theories of criminal behavior • Evaluate a criminal-behavior claim for evidence, limits, and ethical implications • Create a responsible case podcast applying multiple psychological theories Students leave with a completed podcast and a stronger evidence-based framework for analyzing criminal behavior without glamorizing harm.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in psychology, criminal justice, law, media, behavioral science, or ethical storytelling. It fits students who want a rigorous way to examine difficult behavior. Participants should be ready to discuss sensitive topics responsibly, compare competing theories, distinguish explanation from excuse, and create an audio project. Respect for victims, evidence, and classmates’ perspectives is essential. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare major psychological and social theories of criminal behavior • Evaluate a criminal-behavior claim for evidence, limits, and ethical implications • Create a responsible case podcast applying multiple psychological theories Students leave with a completed podcast and a stronger evidence-based framework for analyzing criminal behavior without glamorizing harm.

description_full: What makes a trading decision thoughtful rather than impulsive? This introductory academy gives high school students a clear starting point for exploring financial markets. Students learn basic market vocabulary, see how prices change over time, and use guided chart examples to recognize trends and important price levels. Students read and analyze charts in real time, then use paper trading to practice their new skills without risking real money. They compare possible choices and explain the evidence behind them while exploring how traders prepare, set limits, weigh risk and reward, and review results. Lessons on patience, confidence, fear, and overconfidence show why decision-making habits matter as much as noticing a pattern. As the academy progresses, students create a simple personal framework with rules for preparation, risk, and reflection, along with a journal template for reviewing decisions. The emphasis is on curiosity, responsible thinking, and learning from outcomes, not on easy or guaranteed profits. This two-week Summer Discovery full-day academy takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Learn basic market vocabulary and how price charts show change over time • Read and analyze charts in real time to identify trends and important price levels • Use paper trading to practice new skills without risking real money • Compare market scenarios and explain the evidence behind a decision • Explore how planning, risk, and emotions can shape trading decisions • Create a simple personal framework and journal template for reviewing choices

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the academy, students will be able to: • Explain basic chart terms and recognize simple market trends • Read and analyze charts in real time and use paper trading to practice a rules-based decision • Create clear rules for preparation, risk, and review Students leave with a beginner-friendly framework for studying market decisions and a clearer sense of whether they want to explore finance, economics, or markets further.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are curious about financial markets, economics, finance, or the psychology of decision-making. No prior experience with trading or chart reading is required. It is a good fit for students who enjoy asking why, looking for patterns, working through real examples, and reflecting on their choices. The academy is designed as an introduction, with an emphasis on responsible decision-making, risk awareness, and learning from outcomes.

title: Engineering Research: Scientific Investigation & The Research Process

subject: Engineering

description_full: Good engineering research begins before anything is built. It starts with a question that is specific enough to investigate and important enough to pursue. Students learn how researchers move from a broad interest to a defensible question, a workable method, and a clear plan for gathering evidence. Through literature analysis, research-design exercises, case studies, and proposal workshops, students compare qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods. They practice evaluating source quality, considering ethics, defining variables, and selecting methods that fit an engineering problem. Feedback from peers and the instructor helps students narrow the scope of their ideas and strengthen the logic behind each decision. This hybrid academy combines an on-campus experience with Polygence’s Core Research Program. During the campus program, each student develops an engineering research proposal, abstract, and professional scientific poster, then presents the work in a symposium-style setting. Afterward, students join a virtual cohort and are matched 1:1 with a Polygence research mentor in their field of interest. Across 10 virtual sessions, the mentor helps each student continue the project at an individual pace toward a research paper, symposium presentation, podcast, or another appropriate final format. This two-week Summer Discovery full-day academy takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Narrow a broad engineering interest into a focused research question • Evaluate scientific literature and distinguish stronger from weaker sources • Compare quantitative, qualitative, and mixed research methods • Design a study with appropriate variables, evidence, and ethical safeguards • Draft and revise an abstract, research proposal, and scientific poster • Present the project in a symposium-style session with peer questions • Continue the project through Polygence’s Core Research Program and 10 one-to-one virtual mentor sessions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Formulate a focused engineering research question grounded in existing evidence • Select and justify research methods appropriate to a proposed investigation • Communicate a research plan through an abstract, proposal, poster, and oral presentation Students will leave the campus program with an engineering research proposal and scientific poster, a plan for continuing the project through Polygence mentorship, stronger research and presentation skills, and clearer direction for further study.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are curious about how engineers investigate unanswered questions. It suits students considering engineering, applied science, technology, or design and those who want to test whether research is a good fit before committing to a longer project. No finished research idea is required at the start. Students should be willing to read technical material, refine a question, explain their reasoning, and revise work after feedback. The course is especially useful for students who enjoy asking why a system works, how it could be improved, and what evidence would be needed to support a solution. Students should also be ready to continue after the campus program through 10 one-to-one virtual sessions with a Polygence mentor matched to their field of interest.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Formulate a focused engineering research question grounded in existing evidence • Select and justify research methods appropriate to a proposed investigation • Communicate a research plan through an abstract, proposal, poster, and oral presentation Students will leave the campus program with an engineering research proposal and scientific poster, a plan for continuing the project through Polygence mentorship, stronger research and presentation skills, and clearer direction for further study.

title: Entrepreneurship with NFTE: New Venture Creation
raw_title: Entrepreneurship with NFTE: New Venture Creation
subject: Business, Leadership & Entrepreneurship
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How quickly can a promising idea become a business concept that stands up to questions? Delivered by the Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship in partnership with Summer Discovery, this fast-paced experience guides students from early ideation to a final pitch. Structured activities emphasize clear problem definition, critical thinking, and the ability to ex
description_full: How quickly can a promising idea become a business concept that stands up to questions? Delivered by the Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship in partnership with Summer Discovery, this fast-paced experience guides students from early ideation to a final pitch. Structured activities emphasize clear problem definition, critical thinking, and the ability to explain decisions under time constraints. Short cycles of critique drive the learning. In an Idea Defense Lab, students present early concepts and strengthen the problem, customer, and reasoning behind them. An Investor Feedback Lab shifts the lens to feasibility, differentiation, and business logic. Students apply feedback immediately, refining both the idea and the way they communicate it. A field-based experience connects classroom work with an entrepreneurial environment. Students then synthesize what they have learned, finalize their concept, and prepare for a pitch competition. The final presentation demonstrates how well they can articulate the idea, defend its value, respond to critique, and show meaningful improvement through iteration. This two-week full-day academy takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Generate and clarify an early-stage business idea • Defend the problem and concept in a structured critique • Evaluate feasibility, differentiation, and business logic • Present the idea from an investor’s perspective • Apply feedback through rapid cycles of revision • Deliver a refined concept in a final pitch competition

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Define and articulate a focused business problem and concept • Evaluate and strengthen an idea through market and investor feedback • Deliver and defend a refined entrepreneurial pitch Students leave with a developed business idea, pitch experience, and greater confidence applying feedback to improve their reasoning and communication.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in entrepreneurship, startups, product ideas, business, innovation, or pitching. It fits students who want an active, feedback-driven experience. Participants should be ready to present early work, receive direct critique, revise quickly, and communicate under time constraints. Students do not need to arrive with a finished venture. Curiosity, resilience, and willingness to improve an idea in public will support success. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Define and articulate a focused business problem and concept • Evaluate and strengthen an idea through market and investor feedback • Deliver and defend a refined entrepreneurial pitch Students leave with a developed business idea, pitch experience, and greater confidence applying feedback to improve their reasoning and communication.

title: Forensic Investigation: Crime Scenes & Case Strategy
raw_title: Forensic Investigation: Crime Scenes & Case Strategy
subject: Law & Government
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How does an investigator move from a complicated scene to a defensible conclusion? Students explore crime-scene techniques, tools, and procedures with attention to evidence integrity and chain of custody. They learn how documentation and preservation affect whether later analysis can be trusted. Hands-on work includes fingerprints, fibers, DNA, bloodstain pa
description_full: How does an investigator move from a complicated scene to a defensible conclusion? Students explore crime-scene techniques, tools, and procedures with attention to evidence integrity and chain of custody. They learn how documentation and preservation affect whether later analysis can be trusted. Hands-on work includes fingerprints, fibers, DNA, bloodstain patterns, firearms evidence, toxicology, ballistics, digital forensics, diagramming, sketching, and photography. Students also examine updated procedures for photographic and physical lineups, respectful witness interviewing, and constitutional boundaries when questioning suspects. For the capstone, teams investigate a mock crime scene. They interview a witness, collect and analyze multiple forms of evidence, and compile detailed findings, diagrams, photographs, and logical conclusions into a comprehensive report. A final presentation asks each team to explain its process, interpretation, and evidentiary limits while responding to feedback. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students test their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Document a mock scene through notes, sketches, diagrams, and photography • Preserve evidence and maintain a clear chain of custody • Analyze fingerprints, fibers, DNA, and bloodstain patterns • Examine ballistics, toxicology, and digital evidence • Practice respectful witness interviewing and lineup procedures • Compile and present a comprehensive investigation report

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply foundational crime-scene documentation and evidence-preservation procedures • Analyze multiple evidence types and explain their investigative relevance • Develop and defend a comprehensive crime-scene report Students leave with completed forensic analyses, an investigation report, and a stronger understanding of ethical, scientific, and legal responsibilities in evidence work.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in forensic science, criminal justice, biology, chemistry, digital investigation, or law. It fits students who enjoy careful observation and evidence-based problem-solving. Participants should be ready to follow procedures, document details, work with sensitive scenarios responsibly, collaborate on a mock investigation, and present findings. Patience, accuracy, and respect for witnesses and evidence are essential. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply foundational crime-scene documentation and evidence-preservation procedures • Analyze multiple evidence types and explain their investigative relevance • Develop and defend a comprehensive crime-scene report Students leave with completed forensic analyses, an investigation report, and a stronger understanding of ethical, scientific, and legal responsibilities in evidence work.

title: Introduction to Real Estate
subject: Business, Leadership & Entrepreneurship
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: What does it take to sell a home or manage a residential property? Students build a foundation in real estate while comparing the roles, responsibilities, and daily resources used across the profession. Career exploration introduces the skills behind sales, leasing, property management, contracts, and client communication. Workshops make the process practica
description_full: What does it take to sell a home or manage a residential property? Students build a foundation in real estate while comparing the roles, responsibilities, and daily resources used across the profession. Career exploration introduces the skills behind sales, leasing, property management, contracts, and client communication. Workshops make the process practical. Students practice completing real-estate contracts, distinguish features from benefits, develop a sales pitch, and role-play parts of selling a house. Possible academic field trips which may include a visit to the Weiser Center for Real Estate broaden their view of the industry and the pathways within it. For the capstone, students choose between acting as a real-estate agent selling a home or as a leasing manager running an apartment complex. Teams organize the steps, documents, decisions, and presentation required for their chosen scenario. The project connects professional responsibilities with communication, financial awareness, and the role real estate can play in building wealth. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Explore careers and responsibilities across the real-estate industry • Practice completing introductory real-estate contracts • Distinguish property features from customer benefits • Develop and rehearse a real-estate sales pitch • Role-play steps involved in selling a home • Complete a home-sale or apartment-management capstone

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain major real-estate roles and professional responsibilities • Apply introductory contract and sales concepts to a property scenario • Develop and present a plan to sell a home or manage an apartment complex Students leave with a completed real-estate capstone and a clearer understanding of sales, leasing, property management, and industry careers.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in real estate, business, finance, sales, property management, or how housing can function as an asset. It fits students who want to explore the daily work behind transactions and operations. Participants should be ready to work with contracts, practice client-facing communication, collaborate on a scenario, and present a final project. Organization, curiosity, and willingness to role-play professional decisions will support success.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain major real-estate roles and professional responsibilities • Apply introductory contract and sales concepts to a property scenario • Develop and present a plan to sell a home or manage an apartment complex Students leave with a completed real-estate capstone and a clearer understanding of sales, leasing, property management, and industry careers.

description_full: How do engineers turn physics and material properties into a system that works? Students explore mechanical engineering through structural and materials analysis, design, manufacturing, electricity, thermodynamics, and heat transfer. Lectures connect scientific principles with machines, energy conversion, transportation, and production. Hands-on work moves from foundational experiments to design decisions. Students investigate levers and pulleys, compare materials, build circuits, and test heat transfer and insulation. Simulations and workshops help them connect mathematical or physical models with the behavior of a real system, while peer feedback supports revision. For the capstone, students design and build a functional miniature calorimeter. They move through design, prototype, testing, and improvement milestones while documenting challenges and choices. The final presentation explains the design rationale, integration of physics and thermodynamics, system performance, and changes made after testing. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students test their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Test foundational physics principles through levers and pulleys • Compare materials for structural and design decisions • Build circuits for an introductory mechanical system • Experiment with heat transfer and insulation • Design, prototype, and test a miniature calorimeter • Present system performance and explain design revisions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply physics, materials, electricity, and thermodynamics to engineering problems • Build and test a functional device against defined performance criteria • Explain an iterative design process using evidence from prototype testing Students leave with a functional calorimeter prototype, design documentation, and experience connecting engineering theory with testing and improvement.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend

It fits students who want to build and test a working system. Participants should be ready for quantitative reasoning, hands-on experiments, circuit building, prototype development, troubleshooting, and presentation. Persistence and willingness to learn from failed tests will be valuable. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

title: Medical Research: Scientific Investigation & The Research Process
raw_title: Medical Research: Scientific Investigation & The Research Process
subject: Medicine & Health Sciences
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: A healthcare breakthrough often begins with a carefully framed question. Students choose a topic in medicine or public health, examine what researchers already know, and learn how to turn an area of interest into a focused study that could produce useful evidence. The academy introduces literature review, research ethics, qualitative and quantitative methods
description_full: A healthcare breakthrough often begins with a carefully framed question. Students choose a topic in medicine or public health, examine what researchers already know, and learn how to turn an area of interest into a focused study that could produce useful evidence. The academy introduces literature review, research ethics, qualitative and quantitative methods, data collection, analysis, and community-engaged research. Students practice writing PICO questions, evaluate source quality through a literature scavenger hunt, work through a data challenge, and consider the budget and ethical choices behind clinical research. Abstract and visual-data workshops help them communicate the logic of a study clearly. This hybrid academy combines an on-campus experience with Polygence’s Core Research Program. During the campus program, each student develops a medical research proposal, abstract, and professional scientific poster, then presents the work in a symposium-style setting. Afterward, students join a virtual cohort and are matched 1:1 with a Polygence research mentor in their field of interest. Across 10 virtual sessions, the mentor helps each student continue the project at an individual pace toward a research paper, symposium presentation, podcast, or another appropriate final format. This two-week Summer Discovery full-day academy takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Build a medical research timeline and investigate how evidence develops • Search and evaluate scientific literature for quality and relevance • Formulate a focused research question using the PICO framework • Design a study and address data, budget, and ethical considerations • Write an abstract and create visual material for a scientific poster • Present and defend a proposal in a mock research symposium • Continue the project through Polygence’s Core Research Program and 10 one-to-one virtual mentor sessions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Formulate a researchable medicine or public-health question from scientific literature • Design and justify an ethical study using appropriate methods and data • Communicate and continue a research project through an abstract, poster, oral presentation, and individual mentorship Students will leave the campus program with a medical research proposal and scientific poster, a plan for continuing the project through Polygence mentorship, stronger evidence and communication skills, and clearer direction for further study.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to investigate how medical and public-health knowledge is produced. It fits students interested in medicine, biology, epidemiology, health policy, data, or research and those who want to test an academic interest through a substantial independent proposal. Students do not need a completed research question before arriving. They should be ready to read scientific material, work steadily on one topic, revise after feedback, and discuss ethics with care. The course is a strong fit for students who enjoy asking what evidence supports a healthcare claim and how a better study could answer what remains uncertain. Students should also be ready to continue after the campus program through 10 one-to-one virtual sessions with a Polygence mentor matched to their field of interest.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Formulate a researchable medicine or public-health question from scientific literature • Design and justify an ethical study using appropriate methods and data • Communicate and continue a research project through an abstract, poster, oral presentation, and individual mentorship Students will leave the campus program with a medical research proposal and scientific poster, a plan for continuing the project through Polygence mentorship, stronger evidence and communication skills, and clearer direction for further study.

title: Mock Trial: Courtroom Strategy & Advocacy
subject: Law & Government
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: On the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, students explore courtroom strategy in a lively college-town setting. A trial is a coordinated process in which every role sees the case differently. Students examine the responsibilities of attorneys, defendants, witnesses, judges, and jurors, then study how legal teams prepare a hypothetical case. Jury sel
description_full: On the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, students explore courtroom strategy in a lively college-town setting. A trial is a coordinated process in which every role sees the case differently. Students examine the responsibilities of attorneys, defendants, witnesses, judges, and jurors, then study how legal teams prepare a hypothetical case. Jury selection and voir dire introduce the questions advocates use to understand a potential jury. Working in teams from a mock-trial packet, students develop opening and closing statements, prepare direct and cross-examination questions, and learn when evidence may be introduced or challenged. Practice sessions require them to make objections, respond to an opponent, and revise strategy as the case takes shape. The culminating mock trial puts preparation into motion. Students present arguments, question witnesses, manage exhibits, and respond in real time while maintaining courtroom procedure. Reflection and feedback connect courtroom performance with the critical thinking, problem-solving, teamwork, and public speaking skills that effective advocacy requires. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Analyze the roles of attorneys, witnesses, judges, and jurors • Practice jury selection and the voir dire process • Develop persuasive opening and closing statements • Write direct and cross-examination questions • Introduce evidence and make appropriate objections • Prepare and conduct a collaborative mock trial

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the sequence, roles, and strategic choices within a trial • Construct examinations and arguments from a hypothetical case record • Present and adapt an evidence-based case during a mock trial Students leave with prepared courtroom materials, mock-trial experience, and greater confidence in structured legal advocacy.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in law, debate, justice, acting, public speaking, or strategic problem-solving. It fits students who want to understand both the preparation behind a case and the challenge of presenting it live. Participants should be ready to read a case packet, collaborate closely, take on an assigned role, question witnesses, and speak before classmates. Careful preparation and respectful competition are central to the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the sequence, roles, and strategic choices within a trial • Construct examinations and arguments from a hypothetical case record • Present and adapt an evidence-based case during a mock trial Students leave with prepared courtroom materials, mock-trial experience, and greater confidence in structured legal advocacy.

description_short: How can today’s financial decisions create more options in the future? Students build an introduction to budgeting, saving, credit, debt, investing, and entrepreneurship.
