description_full: How can today’s financial decisions create more options in the future? Students build an introduction to budgeting, saving, credit, debt, investing, and entrepreneurship. They examine compounding, interest rates, stocks, bonds, commodities, and the differences between major exchanges while connecting financial choices to goals, income, time horizon, and personal values. Applied exercises move from concepts to decisions. Students compare the long-term effect of starting to invest at different ages, use simulated money to examine investment preferences, and consider how corporations manage capital. They also study responsible credit, financial integrity, transparency, and the tradeoffs involved in personal or business choices. For the capstone, students develop a personal financial plan individually or with a group. They research a career and realistic salary, set short- and long-term goals, create a monthly budget, plan savings and an emergency fund, explain credit and debt management, and outline an investing strategy. Housing, transportation, and a side-business idea complete the future scenario. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Model how compound interest changes long-term outcomes • Compare stocks, bonds, commodities, and major exchanges • Develop a monthly budget from a researched career salary • Plan savings, an emergency fund, credit, and debt management • Test investment choices using simulated money • Create and present a comprehensive personal financial plan

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how budgeting, credit, debt, saving, and investing connect • Evaluate financial choices using goals, time horizon, and relevant tradeoffs • Develop a realistic long-term personal financial plan Students leave with a completed financial plan and stronger tools for making informed decisions about income, spending, credit, saving, investing, and entrepreneurship.

curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to understand personal finance, investing, credit, budgeting, or entrepreneurship. It fits students who want practical tools they can connect to future goals. Participants should be ready to work with realistic income and expense assumptions, compare choices, use basic calculations, and explain a long-term plan. Careful thinking and willingness to revise assumptions will be valuable. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how budgeting, credit, debt, saving, and investing connect • Evaluate financial choices using goals, time horizon, and relevant tradeoffs • Develop a realistic long-term personal financial plan Students leave with a completed financial plan and stronger tools for making informed decisions about income, spending, credit, saving, investing, and entrepreneurship.

They examine compounding, interest rates, stocks, bonds, commodities, and the differences between major exchanges while connecting financial choices to goals, income, time horizon, and personal values. Applied exercises move from concepts to decisions. Students compare the long-term effect of starting to invest at different ages, use simulated money to examine investment preferences, and consider how corporations manage capital. They also study responsible credit, financial integrity, transparency, and the tradeoffs involved in personal or business choices. For the capstone, students develop a personal financial plan individually or with a group. They research a career and realistic salary, set short- and long-term goals, create a monthly budget, plan savings and an emergency fund, explain credit and debt management, and outline an investing strategy. Housing, transportation, and a side-business idea complete the future scenario. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

description_full: Why do people follow a crowd, obey authority, respond to persuasion, or act differently across social settings? Students examine the forces shaping behavior in groups, relationships, institutions, and daily life. Concepts include conformity, obedience, attribution, social norms, identity, stereotypes, prejudice, gender expectations, and social influence. Classic studies, film and television clips, advertisements, social media, and public moments become material for analysis. Students identify invisible rules, break down the emotional promise behind persuasive messages, and compare research questions, methods, findings, implications, and ethical concerns in studies such as the Bystander Effect and Robbers Cave. For the capstone, students create a podcast examining a trend, public moment, advertisement, scene, social-media behavior, or everyday situation through at least two concepts. They pose a central question, use a vivid example, and explain both what the example shows and what it cannot prove. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students test their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Identify unwritten social norms across everyday settings • Analyze conformity, obedience, attribution, and group identity • Break down persuasive messages and emotional promises • Evaluate classic studies for methods, findings, and ethics • Apply social psychology concepts to media and public behavior • Produce a podcast using two concepts and one central question

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how social context and group processes can shape behavior • Evaluate psychological research and media examples without overstating conclusions • Create a responsible podcast applying multiple social psychology concepts Students leave with a completed podcast and a stronger evidence-based framework for understanding persuasion, conformity, identity, and group behavior.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in psychology, persuasion, group behavior, identity, media, marketing, or social research. It fits students who enjoy examining familiar behavior from a new perspective. Participants should be ready to discuss sensitive social topics respectfully, analyze studies and media, compare concepts, and develop an audio project. Curiosity about both people and evidence will support success. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how social context and group processes can shape behavior • Evaluate psychological research and media examples without overstating conclusions • Create a responsible podcast applying multiple social psychology concepts Students leave with a completed podcast and a stronger evidence-based framework for understanding persuasion, conformity, identity, and group behavior.

description_short: Why is sport both a major business and an important part of American culture? Lectures, discussion, readings, video, and small-group case studies e
description_full: Why is sport both a major business and an important part of American culture? Students survey management issues and strategies shaping the industry, connecting fan participation and consumer behavior with the billions of dollars generated across teams, schools, media, sponsors, and events. Lectures, discussion, readings, video, and small-group case studies examine sports marketing and revenue alongside broader institutional questions. Students consider the financial implications of Title IX, the relationship between sport and race, strategies for reaching Generation Z, and the uniquely American business structure of intercollegiate athletics. Case analysis asks students to connect a management choice with its financial, social, and organizational consequences. The course culminates in a comprehensive assessment of the concepts and readings, requiring students to synthesize how leaders generate revenue while responding to the cultural and institutional responsibilities surrounding sport. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students test their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Examine why sport carries economic and cultural importance • Analyze marketing strategies and influences on consumer behavior • Evaluate revenue and management decisions through case studies • Study the financial implications of Title IX • Discuss the relationship between sport, race, and institutions • Assess the business structure of intercollegiate athletics

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how marketing, consumer behavior, and revenue interact in sports business • Analyze institutional issues such as Title IX, race, and college athletics • Evaluate a sports-management decision using financial and social evidence Students leave with completed case analyses and a stronger framework for understanding the business, cultural, and institutional forces shaping American sports.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in sports business, marketing, finance, college athletics, social issues, or organizational leadership. It fits students who want to understand sport beyond the competition itself. Participants should be ready to read, discuss contested issues respectfully, analyze cases, and connect management decisions with financial and social consequences. No playing experience or prior business coursework is required. Curiosity about the industry behind sport is the strongest fit. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how marketing, consumer behavior, and revenue interact in sports business • Analyze institutional issues such as Title IX, race, and college athletics • Evaluate a sports-management decision using financial and social evidence Students leave with completed case analyses and a stronger framework for understanding the business, cultural, and institutional forces shaping American sports.

title: Anatomy Academy
subject: Medicine & Health Sciences
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How does the structure of a joint shape movement, and how do the body’s systems work together to keep a person functioning? description_full: How does the structure of a joint shape movement, and how do the body’s systems work together to keep a person functioning? Students investigate human anatomy through state-of-the-art 3D models, moving from the nervous, cardiovascular, and lymphatic systems to the respiratory, digestive, urinary, and reproductive systems. The second part of the course brings anatomy into specific regions and professional settings. Students examine the head, neck, trunk, shoulder complex, arms, pelvis, hips, knees, ankles, and feet. Guest lectures from doctors and researchers add specialist perspectives, while a prosthetics demonstration shows how anatomical knowledge informs the design and use of assistive devices. Visits to the Stark Center, Dell Med, the Texas Science and Natural History Museum, and an imaging center help students connect models and classroom concepts with real facilities and technologies. Assignments, review activities, and a final exam reinforce the material. Students also prepare and deliver a PowerPoint presentation that asks them to organize anatomical information and communicate it clearly. This two-week full-day academy takes place at UT Austin. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by the University of Texas at Austin and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Explore the body’s major systems using state-of-the-art 3D anatomical models • Examine the head, trunk, limbs, and major joints by region • Hear guest specialists explain anatomy in medicine and research • Visit medical, imaging, science, and physical-culture facilities • Observe a prosthetics demonstration connecting anatomy with assistive-device design • Prepare and deliver a PowerPoint presentation on an anatomical topic

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Identify major structures across the body’s principal organ systems and regions • Explain relationships between anatomical structure, system function, and human movement • Organize and present anatomical information using models, evidence, and accurate terminology Students will leave with a completed presentation, stronger anatomical and scientific-communication skills, and clearer direction for further study or careers in health, research, or biomedical engineering. Students receive a University of Texas branded certificate of completion at the end of the program.

It is especially relevant for students curious about how anatomical knowledge supports clinical care, medical imaging, rehabilitation, prosthetics, or biomedical engineering. Participants should be ready to study detailed body systems, work with 3D models, learn from guest specialists, take part in facility visits, complete assignments and an exam, and present their work to the class. Applicants must also complete the program application.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Identify major structures across the body’s principal organ systems and regions • Explain relationships between anatomical structure, system function, and human movement • Organize and present anatomical information using models, evidence, and accurate terminology Students will leave with a completed presentation, stronger anatomical and scientific-communication skills, and clearer direction for further study or careers in health, research, or biomedical engineering. title: Biomedical Engineering Academy
subject: Engineering
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How can engineering tools help researchers understand the body or improve healthcare? description_full: How can engineering tools help researchers understand the body or improve healthcare? Students begin with the engineering design process and the major disciplines that contribute to biomedical engineering. Biology and cell and tissue engineering establish a foundation for examining how living systems interact with materials, forces, devices, and data. Each course topic opens a different window into the field. Students investigate biomaterials and biomechanics, then move into computational biomedical engineering, medical devices and instrumentation, organ-on-chip systems, and biomedical imaging. Laboratory tours connect these concepts with current research settings and the equipment biomedical engineers use. Quizzes and short reflection papers ask students to interpret lectures, laboratory activities, tours, and guest presentations. In teams, students prepare two presentations on engineering concepts or research topics. The sequence helps them compare biomedical specialties, communicate technical ideas, and consider the kinds of problems they may want to investigate further. This two-week full-day academy takes place at UT Austin. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by the University of Texas at Austin and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. A supplemental course fee of $195 applies.

curriculum_sections.body: • Compare major engineering disciplines and their roles in biomedical engineering • Explore cell and tissue engineering, biomaterials, and biomechanics • Investigate computational BME, organ-on-chip systems, and biomedical imaging • Examine medical devices and instrumentation used in healthcare research • Tour biomedical engineering laboratories and reflect on research applications • Collaborate on two presentations about engineering concepts and research topics

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how engineering principles apply to biological and medical problems • Compare biomedical engineering specialties, including devices, imaging, materials, and computation • Research and present technical concepts clearly with a team Students will leave with reflection work and team presentations, stronger biomedical-engineering communication skills, and clearer direction for further study or careers in engineering and health technology. description_full: What problem would you solve if you had the chance to do something about it? Students begin with needs they notice in their community or the wider world, then explore how entrepreneurs turn ideas into impact. Starting a company is one path. Creating change inside a school, business, nonprofit, or global organization is another. Working in teams, students use design thinking to generate creative solutions and improve them through conversations with real potential customers. They research their market, build a simple business model, and work through marketing, costs, and pricing. The goal is to move beyond an appealing idea: teams plan and launch a small business by the end of the academy. A UT Austin professor with real-world experience guides the work, joined by guest entrepreneurs and innovators from Austin’s startup scene. Students pitch to real entrepreneurs, listen to feedback, and strengthen their proposals before delivering a final venture pitch in the academy’s own “Shark Tank” competition. Along the way, they practice sharing decisions, leading a team, responding to setbacks, and explaining why their solution matters. This three-week full-day academy for high school students takes place at UT Austin in Austin, Texas, and is developed by the university and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. description_full: Why do some brands earn attention while others disappear into a crowded feed? description_full: A trace of blood, a latent fingerprint, or a single fiber can change the direction of an investigation. Students learn how forensic scientists locate, preserve, test, compare, and interpret physical evidence while protecting it from contamination. Serology exercises introduce screening for biological fluids, and DNA work examines extraction, amplification, profiles, and the role of CODIS in linking cases. The investigation expands into fingerprints, crime-scene photography, documentation, sketches, measurements, firearms evidence, bloodstain patterns, hair, fibers, paint, glass, impressions, digital evidence, drugs, and toxicology. Students practice processing porous and nonporous surfaces, lifting prints, comparing profiles, and using laboratory observations to support conclusions rather than assumptions. Teams apply these methods to two mock crime scenes. They photograph and document the scene, collect and process evidence, prepare sketches, and present their findings. Case discussions and a crime-laboratory tour connect the exercises with laboratory disciplines, expert testimony, and the legal responsibilities that follow when results are reported. description_full: When people disagree about rights, responsibility, or fairness, what gives a legal argument its force? Students examine how the U.S. Constitution, separation of powers, federalism, courts, statutes, and common law organize legal authority. Seminar discussions ask them to identify the legal issue inside a complex public or personal dispute. The course compares civil and criminal systems. Students break down torts, negligence, strict liability, contracts, remedies, property, and intellectual property, then consider criminal culpability and the changing goals of criminal justice. Current events connect these structures with the ways laws and policies affect individuals, families, and communities. A law-school seminar format emphasizes concise readings, active listening, the Socratic method, and lively discussion. Students practice summarizing rules, applying them to new facts, distinguishing moral or political questions from legal ones, and presenting cogent arguments. Negotiation and legislative lawyering add practical perspectives, while sessions on law school and experiential opportunities help students consider future study and public-facing legal work. description_full: Why do some people recover from setbacks more readily than others, and how do emotion, motivation, and relationships shape wellbeing? Students investigate these questions through developmental and positive psychology, examining biological, psychological, social, and environmental influences across the lifespan. The course moves from foundational concepts to the ways psychologists build evidence. Students compare emotional intelligence, personality, temperament, happiness, gratitude, resilience, positive relationships, values, motives, and goals. They learn how curiosity becomes a researchable question, search for scientific articles, and organize findings in a literature review. Quizzes, online discussions, and reflection papers ask students to analyze research rather than accept simple explanations for human behavior. They consider how positive psychology principles can inform personal growth, coping strategies, education, relationships, and mental health while recognizing the limits of broad claims. A final review brings the course’s major themes together and helps students identify questions they may want to pursue further. This three-week high school course takes place at the University of Texas at Austin in Austin, Texas and is available to residential and commuter students. The program is developed by UT Austin and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. description_full: What makes a speaker difficult to ignore? Students begin by identifying what they care about and delivering a short introduction. Work on posture, eye contact, vocal tone, pacing, and purposeful movement shows how an audience reads delivery before evaluating the argument itself. The course then builds persuasive content. Mini-debates and challenge speeches introduce ethos, pathos, and logos, while crossfire practice requires students to answer questions without losing composure or credibility. Audience-adaptation exercises ask students to present the same idea differently to parents, teachers, voters, athletes, gamers, or younger students. Impromptu prompts develop recovery skills under pressure. Each student then writes and rehearses a four-to-six-minute persuasive speech with a hook, problem, argument, solution, call to action, and memorable closing. Peer feedback and dress rehearsals lead to a final showcase. This three-week course takes place at UT Austin. The course is available to residential and commuter students. description_full: A secret message is a mathematical puzzle with a purpose. Students trace cryptography from Caesar shifts and substitution systems to the Enigma machine and the public-key ideas that protect modern communication. Each new cipher reveals both an encoding strategy and a weakness a codebreaker can exploit. Hands-on challenges include building cipher wheels, encrypting and decrypting partner messages, using frequency analysis, and testing Vigenère and Polybius-based systems. Students connect those activities to modular arithmetic, matrices, prime factorization, number theory, and the way computers represent information. Historical cases show how cryptanalysis influenced events and how security standards change when technology advances. For the capstone, students design and analyze an original cryptographic system or complete an in-depth cryptanalysis project. They document the key, method, mathematical reasoning, strengths, limitations, and evidence from testing, then present their findings to the class. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Yale University’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

Students use a problem-spotting challenge to identify everyday frustrations, then apply SCAMPER or “How Might We” brainstorming and an impact-versus-effort matrix to select a promising business idea. The course follows a business and entrepreneurship sequence developed with the Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE). Students create customer personas, design survey or interview questions, study competitors, and craft a value proposition. They organize the problem, solution, and customer segments in a Lean Canvas, then test how well the concept fits the audience it intends to serve. Financial and marketing decisions push the idea further. A pricing simulation introduces revenue streams, cost structures, startup costs, projections, and simplified break-even thinking. Students create a brand name, logo concept, and tagline before building a pitch deck that covers the problem, solution, market, financials, and ask. The course concludes with a polished presentation to a panel, questions from judges, feedback, and reflection. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Yale University’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

Checkpoints guide research, evidence, and presentation so the final project explains both the problem and the microbiological reasoning behind the solution. description_full: Every speech asks an audience to think, feel, do, or remember something. Students learn how informative, persuasive, entertaining, and ceremonial speeches serve those different purposes. They analyze hooks, evidence, stories, tone, pacing, body language, and visuals to see how a speaker earns attention and credibility. Short, low-stakes speaking activities build toward more sustained work. Students tell an impromptu two-minute story, examine professional speeches and advertisements, organize ideas in an outline, and practice vocal delivery and audience awareness. Workshops, structured discussions, and peer critique help them revise both the message and the way they present it. For the capstone, each student develops and delivers a ten-minute speech about a topic they care about. The format may be a demonstration, dramatic reading, persuasive or special-occasion speech, debate, or congressional-style argument. Students research, submit a written outline, rehearse, revise from feedback, and make purposeful choices about how they want the audience to respond. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Yale University’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Compare informative, persuasive, entertaining, and ceremonial speeches • Analyze hooks, evidence, stories, tone, pacing, body language, and visuals • Practice impromptu speaking and audience-focused delivery • Organize research and ideas in a written speech outline • Give and apply specific peer feedback during workshops • Rehearse and deliver a ten-minute capstone speech

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze how rhetorical choices shape a message and audience response • Organize and revise a speech using research, an outline, and feedback • Deliver a sustained presentation with purposeful language and vocal delivery Students leave with a completed speech outline, a ten-minute capstone presentation, rehearsal feedback, and a clearer sense of which forms of communication they may want to explore next.

Curiosity, patience, and a willingness to practice matter more than arriving with polished delivery. Institute for the Gifted eligibility requirements apply, and families must submit a completed program application.

description_full: A new medical technology must do more than sound promising. Students learn to ask what the research shows, which patients may benefit and how cost, access, ethics and public-health effects shape whether an idea can move forward. The course begins with stem-cell biology, clinical evidence and the meaning of sensitivity, specificity and clinical significance. Students debate ownership of cell lines through the story of Henrietta Lacks, map immune responses and study transplantation, blood disorders and CRISPR. A thalassemia genetics game, blood-smear activity and donor-recruitment campaign turn the concepts into applied problems. Organ-system investigations add another layer. Students build lung models, graph heart-rate data, analyze gastrointestinal diseases and decide which patient should receive a kidney using researched policy and evidence. They examine liver-transplant criteria, trace neurological lesions and design a brain prosthetic before serving on a simulated stem-cell ethics board. For the capstone, each student proposes a new use for stem-cell research or another medical technology to address a specific disease. The final presentation must explain the pathophysiology, solution, feasibility, accessibility, public-health implications and future challenges. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Yale University’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Interpret stem-cell research and practice evaluating clinical significance • Debate tissue ownership, transplantation and medical-ethics cases • Model immune responses and investigate blood disorders through genetics activities • Research a CRISPR application and explain its possible medical use • Build organ-system models and analyze heart, lung, kidney, liver and brain cases • Design and present a disease-focused medical technology proposal

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how stem cells and selected medical technologies may address disease • Evaluate research, ethical principles and public-health factors relevant to treatment • Design and defend a medically grounded technology proposal for a specific pathology Students will leave with a course completion certificate, research analyses and a capstone medical-technology proposal, plus greater clarity about continued study in medicine, biotechnology, bioengineering or public health.

curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in medicine, cell biology, genetics, biotechnology or the ethical questions surrounding new treatments. It is especially relevant for students who want to examine how research becomes a clinical application. Students should be ready to work with scientific terminology, interpret evidence, discuss complex cases respectfully and revise a substantial independent project. Students should bring curiosity and care to both the science and its human impact. Students must also meet the Institute for the Gifted eligibility requirements listed in the program FAQ and complete the program application.

description_full: A strong business idea starts with a problem worth solving. Students look for unmet needs, test whether an idea could create real value, and narrow their thinking to one original venture concept. Course content is powered by the Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) and uses NFTE’s nationally recognized curriculum and Entrepreneurial Mindset framework. Students organize their idea with a Lean Business Model Canvas, conduct primary and secondary market research, define a target customer, and estimate demand. Competitive analysis, a SWOT evaluation, and human-centered design help them sharpen their value proposition. Branding and marketing workshops turn that strategy into a message customers can understand. Students then examine fixed and variable costs, pricing, revenue models, unit economics, and break-even points. Using the NFTE Business Workbook and pitch-deck framework, they assemble their research and decisions into a professional presentation. The course culminates in a Fast Pitch Challenge evaluated with NFTE’s official rubric, followed by questions and structured feedback from instructors and experienced entrepreneurs. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Yale University’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Use NFTE’s Entrepreneurial Mindset framework to identify problems and evaluate opportunities • Develop an original venture with a Lean Business Model Canvas • Conduct primary and secondary research to define a target customer • Analyze competitors, complete a SWOT review, and refine a value proposition • Calculate costs, pricing, unit economics, revenue, and a break-even point • Build a pitch deck and compete in NFTE’s Fast Pitch Challenge

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Evaluate a real-world problem as a possible business opportunity • Build and test a venture using a Lean Canvas, market research, and financial evidence • Present and defend an original business concept in NFTE’s Fast Pitch Challenge Students will leave with market research, a completed Lean Canvas, and a professional pitch deck, plus a clearer sense of which parts of entrepreneurship they may want to explore next.

Students should be ready to collaborate, study potential customers, work with basic calculations, revise their thinking, and present to an audience. The course guides students through the NFTE process from identifying a problem to delivering a final pitch. Students must also meet the Institute for the Gifted eligibility requirements listed in the program FAQ and complete the program application.
